odds_why.buffer-zones: Buffer zones are strips of land kept between opposing forces. People do live in some of them, including about 14,000 in the four villages of Cyprus's UN buffer zone and two villages in the Korean demilitarised zone. They live under peacekeepers or military authorities, which leaves no room for a new government. Chernobyl's self-settlers are mostly elderly people whom local officials unofficially let stay. None of these places offers a legal basis for self-rule.
odds_why.combo-religious-status: Religious communities can buy land and form towns under general law, so getting established is common. The US Supreme Court struck down a special school district drawn for one religious group in Kiryas Joel, and a federal judge ruled against Rajneeshpuram in 1985, though Oregon courts later ruled in the city's favour. Colorado City shows long survival followed by state action. Vatican City and Mount Athos rest on old histories that a new group cannot copy, so recognition is close to zero.
odds_why.deep-seabed-area: The deep seabed outside every country's control is called the Area. Article 137 of the Law of the Sea treaty bars any claim to it, and only the International Seabed Authority can issue mining contracts, to operators backed by a member country. The authority's mining rules are still unfinished. Deepsea Ventures, an American company, made a private claim to part of it in 1974, and it is not known to have led to any mining or court ruling.

essays.central-arctic-ocean-and-svalbard:
The Arctic has two very different places that a founder might think about, and it helps to keep them apart. One is the central Arctic Ocean, around the North Pole, which is open sea covered by moving ice. The other is Svalbard, a group of real islands about twice the size of Belgium, where people from many countries can live without a visa. Neither place offers independence.

Begin with the ocean. It is high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control, surrounded by the coastal resource zones of five countries, Canada, Denmark through Greenland, Norway, Russia and the United States. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, applies there, and the same limits apply as on any high seas. No one may claim the water, and a vessel needs a flag or it can be boarded. There is also a treaty on fishing. The Agreement to Prevent Unregulated High Seas Fisheries in the Central Arctic Ocean was concluded at Ilulissat, Greenland, on 3 October 2018 and took effect for Canada on 25 June 2021. Under Articles 1 and 13 it covers the single area of high seas surrounded by those five countries and runs for 16 years, with five-year renewals. Its opening text says ice has generally covered this water all year, though the ice is shrinking.

The seabed below may not be free at all. Under Article 76 of UNCLOS, a coastal country's continental shelf, the seabed it controls for resources, can reach past 200 nautical miles within set limits. The seabed under the central Arctic can therefore belong to a coastal country and fall outside the international deep seabed. Russia's 2007 expedition shows how this works and how it does not. Two small Mir submarines planted a titanium flag on the seabed at the Pole, at 4,261 metres, under the expedition leader Artur Chilingarov. Canada's foreign minister Peter MacKay answered that this was not the 15th century, when countries could plant flags and claim territory, and a US State Department spokesman said the flag had no legal standing. Lindsay Parson of Britain's National Oceanography Centre explained that the 200-nautical-mile zones of the five coastal countries leave a central area of about 300,000 to 400,000 square kilometres in question, which is an unofficial figure. He said any country wanting that seabed has to build a scientific case under the treaty, and he called the dive a scientific achievement that meant very little as a legal claim. A private flag would have no more effect. Greenpeace lowered its own flag to the same seabed in April 2013, with a capsule holding nearly three million signatures asking for a global sanctuary. The European Parliament has called for a sanctuary too, and none has been created.

The scientific process has moved on since the 2007 dive. The Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf is the UN expert body that reviews these cases. On 6 February 2023 it issued recommendations on Russia's Arctic submission, agreeing that the Lomonosov Ridge, the Mendeleev-Alpha Rise and the Podvodnikov Basin are natural extensions of Russia's shelf and finding its evidence on the Gakkel Ridge insufficient. Russia filed a revised submission on 14 February 2023. Denmark for Greenland and Canada filed their own Arctic submissions in 2013 to 2014 and in 2019, which the commission had not yet considered as of March 2023, and they run towards the same area near the North Pole. The commission does not settle overlaps, so the countries have to negotiate them, and the coastal country sets its own final limits. Any seabed left beyond the final boundaries would be the international deep seabed, run by the International Seabed Authority.

Physically, the ocean is very hard to live on. It offers moving ice and no local supplies. The one legal test comes from a research camp. T-3, a drifting iceberg about 11 by 5 kilometres, was a staffed American station from 1952 until the last station closed on 1 October 1974. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla shot and killed the station manager, Bennie Lightsey, during a dispute over raisin wine. The island lay within the sector Canada claimed, and Canada took no action. American officials flew him to Virginia and tried him under the special American law for crimes at sea. A jury convicted him of involuntary manslaughter. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, split evenly on whether American law applied there, so the trial court's ruling stayed in place, and it overturned the conviction for other trial errors. He was acquitted at a new trial. Congress settled the question of legal authority over such a place in 1984. Living on the ice therefore did not put anyone beyond a court.

Now turn to Svalbard. Until the 20th century it was terra nullius, land belonging to no state. Whalers and then miners from many countries worked there with almost no law, and disputes between miners and owners created demand for a government. The 1920 Svalbard Treaty was the answer, signed in Paris on 9 February 1920 and in force from 14 August 1925. It began with 14 parties and has 49 members as of 2026, according to Wikipedia. Article 1 recognizes Norway's "full and absolute sovereignty". Articles 2 and 3 give nationals of member countries equal rights to fishing, hunting, access, trade and mining, subject to local law. Article 8 says taxes must be spent on Svalbard itself, and mining rules cannot favor anyone. Article 9 says no naval base or fortification may be built. Russia uses its rights through its settlements at Barentsburg and Pyramiden, and about 2,500 people live on the islands.

Many people hear "no visa" and assume Svalbard is a kind of free zone. The Governor of Svalbard, Norway's local official, explains otherwise. Norway's Immigration Act does not apply there, so a foreigner needs no Norwegian visa or residence permit, though someone needing a Schengen visa must have one to travel through mainland Norway, and a double-entry visa to come back. Everyone must carry a valid travel document. Under Norway's rejection and expulsion regulations for Svalbard, people must have the means to live there, and the Governor may reject those who do not. This applies to Norwegians and foreigners alike. Those planning to come are advised to obtain work and housing first. Most housing belongs to employers, so it is hard to get housing without a job. The Norwegian state owns practically all land, and in practice it is not possible to buy a plot to build a home. Private boats and planes must send advance notice of passengers and crew. Living there gives no rights to govern. Norwegian law and the Governor apply. Under rules announced in 2022, non-Norwegians must have lived three years in a Norwegian municipality to vote or stand in Longyearbyen's local elections, and time on Svalbard does not count, which could affect over 700 of the 2,500 people there.

Suppose a group of friends moved to Longyearbyen, the main town, and announced a self-governing community. They would need jobs and homes from existing employers, and they could rent and trade like anyone else. Their declaration would have no effect, because 49 countries have recognized Norway's sovereignty in the treaty. If they could not support themselves, the Governor could send them away.

Older Arctic cases show what happens to those who try to take land. Norway itself tried in 1931 to occupy part of eastern Greenland, calling it Erik the Red's Land and arguing it belonged to no state. On 5 April 1933 the Permanent Court of International Justice ruled for Denmark by twelve votes to two and found the proclamation unlawful and invalid. In 1921 Vilhjalmur Stefansson sent five settlers to Wrangel Island, north of Siberia, to claim it for Canada. A relief ship failed in 1922, three set out for Siberia and vanished, one died of scurvy, and Ada Blackjack survived alone until rescue in August 1923. A new party of 13 was removed by a Soviet ship in 1924, and its leader, Charles Wells, and two children died. Hans Island, a bare rock of 1.3 square kilometres, was divided peacefully by Canada, Denmark and Greenland on 14 June 2022 after decades in which each side raised flags and left gifts.

The workable version is simple and limited. An ordinary person from a member country can move to Svalbard, if they can support themselves, and live and do business under Norwegian law. In the central ocean, a registered ship or a government-backed camp is possible for short periods. The legal estimate for this zone is moderate because of those open rights, and the holding estimate is low because no one can govern there.
essays.floating-ice:
Ice that floats in the sea is hard for the law to classify. A person can walk on it and build a hut, as on land, and it also moves with the currents and melts. Who owns a floating iceberg has no settled answer.

It helps to separate three kinds of floating ice. Sea ice forms when the ocean surface freezes. An ice shelf is a thick sheet of floating ice still attached to land, like those around Antarctica. An iceberg or ice island is a large piece that has broken off a glacier or shelf and drifts free.

Legal writers take three views of an iceberg floating free. The first says it belongs to no one, which lawyers call res nullius, so the first to take it may keep it, much as a fisherman keeps a fish. The second says it can be held under a claim by a country. The third says it is shared by all, which is called res communis, in the way the open sea is shared. In a 2022 article in the law journal Ius Novum, Mateusz Osiecki argues that an iceberg floating free in Antarctic waters is no country's property and sits on the high seas, so taking and towing it would probably not breach any country's territorial rights. That is one writer's reasoning, and no court has ruled on it. C. Wood-Donnelly, writing in Marine Policy in 2022, describes iceberg harvesting as unregulated and its legal status in international law as limited to the "rule of capture", which is close to the first view.

Nearer the coast the answer is firmer. Matthew Paterson, writing in 2019, says icebergs in a territorial sea fall under the coastal country's laws, and he suggests that in the wider resource zone they may count as natural resources under its sovereign rights. Canada is the one state he found regulating them. In Newfoundland and Labrador, six companies were reported to hold licences, paying the province a fee based on volume after locals objected to a flat $5,000 charge. Paterson also argues that Article 7 of the 1991 Environmental Protocol, which bars mineral resource activities in Antarctica other than scientific research, could stop commercial harvesting there if "mineral" is read in its scientific sense, and he notes that the dictionary sense makes this debatable.

Location adds another layer. The Antarctic Treaty, under its Article VI, covers everything south of 60 degrees South, including all ice shelves, without taking away rights any country has on the high seas in that area. An ice shelf is therefore treated like part of Antarctica, with its frozen claims and its rules. Paterson, citing the writer Joyner, suggests that a shelf frozen to the seabed should be treated as land and otherwise as part of the sea. A berg that has drifted north of that line is simply floating in the ocean. A towing ship answers to the country whose flag it flies. Osiecki notes that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has joined neither the Antarctic Treaty System nor the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, which leaves open how far those rules bind a UAE-flagged tow. He also sets out the duties under the 1991 Environmental Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty.

The one court that has come near this question did so after a killing. T-3, also called Fletcher's Ice Island, was a drifting iceberg in the Arctic Ocean, about 11 by 5 kilometres, used as a staffed American research station from 1952 until the last station closed on 1 October 1974, with huts, a power plant and an airstrip. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla, armed with a borrowed rifle during a dispute over raisin wine, shot and killed the station manager, Bennie Lightsey. The island then lay in the Arctic sector Canada claimed, but Canada chose not to act and said this did not affect its claims. American officials flew Escamilla to Virginia and charged him, arguing that the ice was on the high seas and so within the special American law for crimes at sea. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, split evenly on whether American law covered an unclaimed ice island, so the trial court's ruling stayed in place. The conviction was overturned for other errors, and he was acquitted at a new trial. Congress did not settle the question until a change to federal law in 1984. The shooting on unclaimed ice did not fall outside all law. A national government took the suspect home, and the argument was about which statute applied.

Physically, the record shows that people can live on ice for weeks or years with heavy support, and never permanently. On 21 May 1937 the Soviet Union set up North Pole-1 on a floe about 20 kilometres from the Pole. Four men lived there for nine months while the floe drifted 2,850 kilometres, until icebreakers took them off in February 1938. From 1954, one to three stations ran each year. A typical camp began in April and lasted two or three years, until its floe reached the Greenland Sea, and North Pole-22 drifted for nine years. Some 800 people have drifted on these stations since 1937, with crews replaced each year. All were run by one government body, the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute. From the mid-2000s it became hard to find a safe floe, and several stations were evacuated early because the ice thawed too fast. Russia therefore ordered a self-propelled, ice-resistant platform in 2017, completed in August 2022, which ran station NP-41 from 2022 to 2024 and started NP-42 in 2024.

Antarctic ice has given its own warning. The iceberg A23a broke from the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in 1986 and carried off part of the Soviet base Druzhnaya I, which stood on that part of the shelf. Rusted debris from the base could still be seen in the ice in January 2025. A23a measured about 3,500 square kilometres in January 2025, when it was the largest iceberg in the world. By March 2026 it was down to 180 square kilometres, and by July 2026 it was thought to be gone or nearly so.

Suppose a private group sets up on a floe and declares it a country. The first thing it needs is an aircraft or ship, and the base for that is in some country. Camp Barneo shows what follows. It was a private tourist camp near the North Pole, founded in 2002 by the Russian Alexander Orlov, with visits from about $20,000. Because the ice keeps moving, it had to be rebuilt from nothing every April, and in 2007 winds pushed it at 0.8 kilometres an hour. Every trip from 2002 to 2017 started and ended at Longyearbyen on Svalbard, so it relied on Norway. In 2016, after Chechen paratroopers held military exercises at Barneo, Norway imposed a flight ban, which it later lifted. A Russia-Ukraine dispute stopped tourist flights in 2019, COVID-19 cancelled two seasons, Russia's invasion of Ukraine ended plans for 2022, and a 2024 season was cancelled. The camp last operated in 2018. No one needs to board the ice to stop a camp, because restricting the flights is enough.

The other bumps follow from that. A camp without a government behind it has no icebreaker to rescue it when the floe cracks. Its residents remain citizens of their home countries, with the same taxes and the same criminal law. It has no fixed address for a bank, an insurer or a land title, since the ground itself drifts and may melt. The Montevideo Convention, the 1933 treaty that defines a state, asks for a defined territory, which a melting floe struggles to offer.

Building a stronger iceberg has been tried on paper. Project Habakkuk was a British wartime plan by Geoffrey Pyke for a floating airbase made of ice. Max Perutz warned in 1942 that natural icebergs have too little surface above water for an airstrip and can roll over. The idea moved on to pykrete, a frozen mix of water and wood pulp, and a ship 600 metres long. Pykrete sagged unless cooled to minus 16 degrees Celsius, the estimate rose from £700,000 to £2.5 million, and the board called the ship impractical in December 1943. The UAE Iceberg Project, announced in 2017 by Abdulla Alsheni at an estimated $100 to 150 million, aimed only to tow a berg from near Heard Island to Fujairah for water, and no tow is known to have taken place.

The workable version is a temporary camp or research station with a country or a large company behind it, supplied by air or ship, lasting a season to a few years. It gives no title and no self-rule. Estimates put the chance of building a lasting place very low, while the legal estimate is moderate only because the law is unsettled.
essays.buffer-zones:
When two armies stop fighting, they often agree to pull back from each other and leave a strip of land between them, so that a stray shot or a patrol does not restart the war. That strip is a buffer zone. Because no army is meant to hold it, it can look on a map like land that belongs to nobody, and people interested in empty places sometimes wonder whether a new territory could be set up there. It cannot, and the reasons say a good deal about how ceasefires work. The surrounding countries, or the parties to the ceasefire, keep their claims. A peacekeeping force or a ceasefire body controls entry. The strip is an arrangement between the two sides, and the land inside still belongs to someone in law.

The Korean Demilitarized Zone is the most guarded example. It was created by the armistice, or ceasefire agreement, of 27 July 1953. Under it, each side moved back 2,000 metres from the front line, leaving a zone about 4 kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long. Only two villages are allowed to remain inside. Daeseong-dong, also called Tae Sung Dong or Freedom Village, is on the southern side, governed and protected by the United Nations Command. It had 218 people in 2008, descended from those who owned the land before the war. They must generally spend at least 240 nights a year there to keep their residency. They count as South Korean citizens and do not pay tax or do military service. Kijŏng-dong, or Peace Village, is on the northern side. Only North Korea or the UN Command can give access. In January 2026 the UN Command strongly opposed South Korean bills that would give Seoul authority over non-military entry, calling them completely at odds with the armistice and stressing its role as the zone's administrator. If South Korea's own lawmakers meet that response, a private founder has little room. Those villagers' special position comes from the armistice and from their families' earlier ownership of the land. A newcomer has no route in, and the edges of the zone are among the most heavily armed borders in the world.

The UN Buffer Zone in Cyprus, also called the Green Line, shows a much more lived-in version. It began in 1964 and was extended after the ceasefire of 16 August 1974, which followed the Turkish invasion and split the island. It runs 180 kilometres across the island and covers 346 square kilometres, ranging from under 20 metres wide in places to over 7 kilometres, and it cuts through the capital, Nicosia. The UN force in Cyprus patrols it. Four villages lie inside it. Their listed populations in 2021 were Athienou 9,721, Pyla 2,771, Troulloi 1,175 and Deneia 373, about 14,000 people in all. Pyla is the only village, by the UN force's account, where Greek and Turkish Cypriots live side by side. The UN divides the zone into two kinds of ground. In the Civil Use Areas, which include these villages, people may enter freely. Everywhere else, civilian activity needs specific authorisation from the UN force, which weighs security, ownership and its own operations when dealing with civilian building. It handles about 1,000 incidents a year. These are people who were already there, or their descendants, and they remain citizens of an existing country. Crossing was very limited until April 2003, when the Turkish Cypriot administration eased its restrictions after nearly 30 years.

A person might assume that such a mixed village, in a place neither side fully governs, would be a good place to declare something new. No one has been reported trying to declare a separate state in the zone, and small events show how closely the ground is watched. In 2009 UN troops stopped villagers in Mammari, a Civil Use Area, from gathering wild asparagus in nearby fields, saying the fields were in a restricted area near Turkish military outposts. Access to restricted ground required a request to the UN. In August 2023 de facto Turkish security forces attacked UN peacekeepers near Pyla in a dispute over unauthorised construction, seriously injuring three, and the Security Council called it a violation of the status quo, meaning the existing situation that is meant to stay unchanged. In 1996 two Greek Cypriot protesters were killed during protests against the division, one beaten and one shot while climbing a flagpole. A newcomer's building or flag would land in that setting, and it would need authorisation from a force whose job is to prevent changes.

The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone is a different kind of no-go strip. It was emptied because of radiation, with no army line involved. The 30-kilometre zone in Ukraine and Belarus was evacuated after the 1986 nuclear disaster, about 100,000 people in all. About 1,200 people returned in 1986. They are called samosely, meaning self-settlers. Most were elderly people who had lived there before the disaster. Many had been told they could go home in a few days, and they then faced discrimination in the areas where they were resettled. Some outsiders came too. Ukraine's government has not legalised their settlements, because living in the zone remains prohibited. A bill backed by Ukraine's parliament at first reading in July 2021 proposed fines of 17,000 to 42,500 hryvnia or restriction of freedom for illegal entry, and whether it passed in that form is not known. A minister said in 2013 that they receive full social support, and local officials have unofficially let elderly settlers stay.

The samosely show what tolerance looks like. Officials look away because the people are old, few and doing no harm, and because the state already pays them social support. They depend on the same state for help, which leaves them far from independent. Their number has fallen mainly through old age, from 314 in a 2007 census to 135 in 2017, and a Ukrainian report in April 2026 put the number left at about 25. Russian forces occupied the area in 2022, and residents have described that time as frightening. None of them has declared a separate state, and they remain residents of the countries that run the zone.

Several misunderstandings are worth clearing up. One is that a ceasefire strip is a gap in sovereignty, the legal right to rule a place. A ceasefire only pauses a fight, and the claims remain in place on both sides. The UN General Assembly's Friendly Relations Declaration of 1970 says this in its own way. States must not use force to violate international lines of demarcation such as armistice lines, and that duty does not affect the parties' positions on the status of those lines. Another is that peacekeepers are a kind of government that could be persuaded to let a project go ahead. Their job is to keep the two sides apart under the terms given to them, and they have no power to give away land. A third is that a place with no tax, like the Korean village, is free of the state. Its residents hold those exemptions because of special rules from an armistice, and they are still South Korean citizens. A fourth is that physical emptiness means legal emptiness. Chernobyl has been sealed for 40 years, and two governments still run it.

The risks of trying are serious. In the Korean zone, entry without permission means walking into a military frontier. In Cyprus, unauthorised activity outside the Civil Use Areas meets UN patrols, and the 2023 clash at Pyla shows how quickly construction can involve armed forces. At Chernobyl, living in the zone is prohibited, and the radiation that emptied it remains a health issue for anyone new.

There is no way to set up a self-governing territory here. The realistic options are to study or visit where that is allowed, and to work with those trying to reduce tension, such as the bicommunal life of Pyla. People do live in these zones, under peacekeepers or military authorities, and that leaves no room for a new government. For that reason the chances of building something are put at about 10 percent, law and holding at the same low level, and recognition at a tenth of a percent. Nothing in the known record gives a legal basis for self-rule in such a place.
essays.combo-treaty-buffer-land:
Buffer zones exist because two sides have stopped fighting without settling who owns what, and a strip of land is kept between them. Some people see these as gaps in the world's map. This route asks whether a treaty could turn such a strip, or a demilitarised area, into a place for a community or a special regime. It combines a buffer zone with international agreement and a host's consent.

The first thing the law settles is that a buffer is not empty of claims. The UN Buffer Zone in Cyprus, 346 square kilometres, was set by ceasefire, and the UN patrols it without owning it, while the claims of the governments on either side continue. Korea's Demilitarized Zone, about 250 kilometres long and 4 wide, comes from the armistice of 27 July 1953. Two villages remain inside it by decision of the armistice committee. Daeseong-dong on the southern side is protected by the United Nations Command, and its 218 residents in 2008 were South Korean citizens who paid no tax and did no military service, on condition that they spend 240 nights a year there. A person arriving there could not join them, since residence descends from pre-war landowners. Pyla in Cyprus is a mixed village in the zone, and about 14,000 people live in the four villages of the Cyprus zone, by listed populations for 2021.

A peace treaty can do more. The Israel and Jordan treaty of 1994 recognised Jordanian sovereignty at Baqura, also called Naharayim or the Island of Peace, and it gave Israeli landowners who had held the land since before 1948 a special regime with free entry, under a lease of 25 years, automatically renewed unless one side gave a year's notice. Jordan gave that notice in October 2018 and took full control on 10 November 2019. The Åland Islands are the longest-running peaceful example of demilitarisation. They are neutral under a 1921 convention and part of Finland. The Free Territory of Trieste was the grand design, to be a neutral country under the UN Security Council, and it never got past military governors before Italy and Yugoslavia divided it in 1954.

Now the open points. Nobody has decided whether a third party could administer a demilitarised strip for residents under a new treaty, because no one has asked. In Moresnet and Brčko, a joint regime emerged from a dispute, and each was the work of the parties. Reading the examples, it seems that any such regime needs consent from both of the parties whose quarrel made the buffer. Those parties have often not been able to agree on more basic things. No case has tested whether the UN or another body could accept such a job for a private community.

Follow it step by step. A private group arriving in a UN buffer zone would be stopped by peacekeepers or by the armed forces at the edges. In Korea, the edges of the zone are among the most heavily armed borders in the world. Suppose the two parties wanted a neutral project, say a peace park or a free economic zone. A founder would need both to sign, and a treaty term with an end date or a notice clause, of the kind Jordan used. Investors and insurers would see that one bad year in relations could shut it. Its residents would keep their nationality, its goods would have to pass through one or both sides' customs, and any bank would look to those two states. If the regime ended, private rights would rest on whatever the treaty says. At Baqura, Jordan took full control when the regime ended, whatever the earlier ownership of the land.

The potential is low, and it is tied to peace-making. The strongest version is a treaty that ends a dispute and includes a special area, with clear rights for those already on the land, under a body both sides trust. Such a place could bring real benefit to its people. A founder's role in it would be small, as a contractor or investor at most, and the sovereignty questions would be settled by the two states.
essays.taking-over-a-state-or-town:
This route starts from something that already exists. Instead of looking for empty water or unclaimed rock, a group tries to take over a government that is already running, either a country's or a town's. The land stays where it is, owned and governed by the same existing country or local government. There are two very different ways to try this. One is to move people in and vote. The other is armed force, usually by mercenaries, meaning soldiers for hire.

A town is a unit of local government. It gets its powers from the state or country around it, and those powers cover local matters such as the town budget, local services and, in many places, the use of land. Moving to a town and voting there is ordinary legal behaviour. Suppose a few hundred people move into a town of about a thousand and elect a majority of its council. They can then cut the budget and change local rules. The next morning, state law, national law, the courts and the tax office apply as they did before. Voters and courts in a town can only change what local government controls, and a council has no power over criminal law, passports or the country's borders.

The first bump is getting enough people to come. The Free State Project, a plan for libertarians (people who favour very limited government) to move to New Hampshire, began in 2001 with an article by Jason Sorens that proposed an independent libertarian nation or, failing that, concessions from the US government. Sorens calculated that 20,000 people moving to one small state could change it. Pledges reached 20,000 on 3 February 2016, and by May 2022 about 6,232 people had moved. In the 2017 to 2018 term, Free Staters held 17 of the 400 seats in the state House of Representatives. A movement called NH Exit Now, formed in 2026, calls for secession, and New Hampshire remains a US state. In Texas v. White in 1869 the US Supreme Court held that a state cannot secede on its own, with no way out "except through revolution or through consent of the States".

The second bump is daily life and cost. A smaller attempt, the Free Town Project, began in 2004 when a splinter group chose Grafton, New Hampshire, for its lack of zoning laws (rules on how land may be used) and its very low property tax. No records were kept of how many came. The population rose from 1,138 in 2000 to 1,340 in 2010, with nearly all the newcomers men, many living in yurts, trailers, tents and shipping containers. They voted through a 30% cut in the small town budget and removed funding for the county's senior citizens' council. Lawsuits they filed to set legal precedents raised the town's costs.

The third bump is the neighbours, and then the higher authorities. The largest case is Rajneeshpuram in Oregon. In 1981 followers of the Indian spiritual teacher Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh bought the 64,281-acre Big Muddy Ranch for $5.75 million and within three years had built a city of up to about 7,000 people. The nearest town, Antelope, had under 60 people. Its residents voted in April 1982 on dissolving the town to avoid a takeover, and the followers had enough votes to defeat the plan. In May 1982 the ranch voted to become a city. Oregon's attorney general argued that the new city merged church and state, and a land-use group argued that it broke land-use law. Federal Judge Helen Frye ruled against the city in the church-and-state suit in late 1985, too late to matter, and that ruling was not contested. The Oregon Court of Appeals ruled in 1986 that the incorporation had not broken the state's agricultural land goals, and the Oregon Supreme Court closed the litigation in 1987, which left the city vacant and bankrupt but legal under Oregon law.

Criminal cases brought the project down before those lawsuits were settled. In 1984 some leaders deliberately spread disease to lower turnout in county elections, sickening 751 people and sending 45 to hospital, and a plot to kill the US attorney for Oregon followed. Rajneesh, accused of immigration violations, entered a plea without admitting guilt and agreed to leave the country. The commune broke up in 1985.

Armed takeover is a crime in the places involved, and foreign governments, police and informers have usually stopped it early. The first obstacle is money. For the 1981 attempt in Seychelles, an island country in the Indian Ocean, the mercenary Mike Hoare advised raising $5 million, and $300,000 was found. The second is secrecy, because people must be hired and weapons moved. In Operation Red Dog, a 1981 plot by white supremacists against Dominica in the Caribbean, about $70,000 was collected, and the replacement boat captain, Michael Howell, went to the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms. On 27 April 1981 nine men were arrested at a New Orleans marina as they prepared to board, with three undercover agents in the group. US law punishes preparing, from within the United States, a military expedition against a country at peace with it, with up to three years in prison (18 USC 960). In Seychelles, a security officer at the airport found an AK-47 in the bag of one of the 53 men.

The third is the law of every country along the way. After the Seychelles gunfight, most of the mercenaries hijacked an Air India airliner to Durban. South Africa, which had encouraged the plot, charged them under its aviation law over the hijacking and not over the coup attempt, and 34 served about four months. Hoare himself got ten years and was released in May 1985 under an amnesty, after about three. Seychelles sentenced four captured men to death, and all six prisoners were pardoned after talks and a $3 million payment. In the Wonga Coup of 2004 against Equatorial Guinea, police at Harare airport in Zimbabwe impounded a Boeing 727 with 64 former soldiers and arrested Simon Mann, who served three years in Zimbabwe and was then sentenced in Equatorial Guinea to more than 34 years, until a pardon in 2009.

Bob Denard is often taken as proof that this works. He landed in the Comoros in 1978 with 43 men, overthrew Ali Soilih and for 11 years ran a 500-strong presidential guard under President Abdallah. He held power through a recognised president and founded nothing new, and witnesses at his later trial said French intelligence had supported him. After Abdallah was shot in 1989 Denard left, and when he landed again in 1995 the French army ended the attempt within about a week. A French court later convicted him. He is the one long-lasting case, and his control ended as well.

South Africa's apartheid government declared four homelands, or Bantustans, independent between 1976 and 1981, after the Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 made every Black South African a citizen of one, while saying they stayed South African citizens for purposes of international law. Apart from South Africa and the four themselves, which recognised one another, no government recognised them, so a government's own declaration settled nothing abroad, and they were absorbed back in 1994. Slab City in California, a camp of about 4,000 people in winter and 150 in summer on a former Marine base, has no local government, but California and US law still apply, though they are largely not enforced there.

The most workable version is the open one, and Marinaleda in Spain is its longest example. Landless farm workers there formed the Workers' Unity Collective, won 9 of 11 council seats in 1979 and kept the same mayor until 2023. After a hunger strike in 1980 and a 30-day occupation in 1984, 1,200 hectares of a duke's farm were handed over for local use in 1991. Critics say almost 66% of its income comes from higher levels of government. It remains an ordinary Spanish municipality under Spanish law. The voting route can win local offices and change how a place lives, for as long as the voters stay and the laws above allow it, and final authority stays where it was. Recognition as a new country by this route is close to nil.
essays.combo-treaty-cession-new-body:
The cleanest legal route to a new territory would be this. An existing state signs a treaty handing a piece of its land to a new body, gives up all claim to it, and the new body becomes its government. Title would then come from the one party entitled to give it. This combines buying from a state, an agreement between governments, and the attempt to become a state.

Some of this is clear. States can transfer territory to each other. Egypt announced in 2016 that it would hand Tiran and Sanafir to Saudi Arabia and ratified the treaty in 2017, although the handover has stalled and sources differ on where it stands. Sovereignty over Vatican City was recognised to the Holy See by Italy in the Lateran Treaty of 1929, creating a state of 44 hectares. It is also clear that treaties are made between entities with capacity. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, in Article 6, says every state has the capacity to make them. It says nothing that helps a company or club. And it is clear that a transfer from one state does not bind other states to recognise the result. South Africa declared four homelands independent from 1976, starting with Transkei, and apart from South Africa and the four themselves, which recognised one another, no government accepted them.

The hard part is the recipient. The Holy See was an old international body with diplomatic ties before 1929, and its case is not a pattern for a new group. The closest modern parallel is the 1998 treaty by which Malta gave the Order of Malta, another old body with diplomatic ties, use of part of Fort St Angelo for 99 years. It gave the Order use with listed privileges and it did not give sovereignty. What is open, and has not been tested, is whether a brand-new private body could receive sovereignty directly by treaty. Nothing in the Vienna Convention says that it could never hold title, since a place may become a state by meeting the usual tests of territory, population and government. Reading the text, it seems that a treaty signed with a body that is not yet a state would at first count as a domestic act of the giving state or as a private contract, and that the new place's status would depend on other governments' responses. That reasoning is a reading and no court has ruled on it.

Politics makes the transfer far harder than the law. In the Tiran and Sanafir case, a transfer between two friendly states set off the largest protests of the Egyptian president's time in office, with hundreds arrested. The Chagos treaty shows how slow it can be, even when a court has spoken. In 2019 the International Court of Justice advised that Britain should end its rule of the islands. On 22 May 2025 Britain and Mauritius signed a treaty transferring sovereignty and letting Britain exercise rights on Diego Garcia for an initial 99 years, for annual payments. Then a change in the American position stalled it, the British bill lapsed in April 2026, and as of October 2026 it was not in force. The same opinion shows a further limit. The court held that Mauritius's agreement to give up the islands in 1965 was not valid, because it came while Britain ruled Mauritius, and that land cannot be split off without the free and genuine will of the people concerned. Reading that reasoning, a founder would have to expect the people on any ceded land to have a say, and a deal that ignored them would be open to attack.

Follow the steps. A government must first want this, which means something large in exchange and few voters who object. Its constitution may forbid giving up land, as the Honduran Supreme Court said of an earlier special zone plan on grounds of sovereignty. A parliament must vote, and a later government may attack the treaty. Neighbours with interests in the area would then respond. If it all succeeded, the new place would hold land and would need everything else, including a passport other states accept, a country code, a bank that will deal with it and recognition. The founders would remain citizens of their home countries, with those countries' tax and criminal laws still following them, until they gave up that nationality.

It has potential only as a very rare event. The strongest version would be a state already willing to give up a remote, unpopulated and undisputed piece of land, to a body with real backing from other governments, perhaps as part of a settlement of a bigger problem. No such transfer to a new private body has taken place in modern times. If one did, the title would be strong, which explains the high legal and holding figures.
essays.buy-from-a-state:
Buying a house and buying a country sound like larger and smaller versions of the same act. In law they are two different things. When someone buys land, they get ownership, which is the right to use it, fence it and sell it. The right to make the laws on that land, run its courts and collect its taxes is a separate thing called sovereignty, and it stays with the government. A person who owns a whole island still pays that country's taxes. The two can move separately. A classic American Journal of International Law article by Sayre explains that when a territory changes rulers, private owners generally keep their land while political authority passes to the new ruler. Sovereignty moves only when one government agrees to hand it to another, normally by treaty. So the selling country keeps authority until a treaty moves it to the buyer.

Countries have done this many times. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, about 2,140,000 square kilometres. It paid Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867, about 1,717,856 square kilometres. It paid Denmark $25 million in 1916 for the 400 square kilometres of the Danish West Indies. Pakistan bought Gwadar from Muscat and Oman in 1958, at a price given as about £3 million or 5.5 billion Pakistani rupees. The most recent sale on Wikipedia's list of such purchases came in 1963, when West Germany paid the Netherlands 280 million Deutsche Marks for Elten, Selfkant and Suderwick. Every buyer and seller on that list is a country or a country-like ruler, and the list leaves out leases. A private buyer has no treaty partner, because a treaty is an agreement between states.

The first obstacle is that a government has to be willing to sell, and governments almost always refuse. The United States has tried to buy Greenland several times, including a secret offer of $100 million in gold in 1946, which Denmark rejected. When President Trump raised it in 2019, the Danish prime minister called the idea absurd. Under section 21 of Greenland's Self-Government Act, independence is for the Greenlandic people to decide, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum, so the decision does not rest with one government alone. A September 2026 security agreement involved no sale. Sultan Abdul Hamid II told Theodor Herzl in 1896 that he could not sell a foot of land.

Private attempts have gone the same way. The founders of Minerva and Operation Atlantis looked for a government willing to sell and found none. Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman whose Romanov Empire project issued passports online, talked with several countries, and as of 2017 his talks with Kiribati and the Gambia had failed. Freedonia tried to lease land in Somaliland in 2001 and was rejected. No private purchase in the 20th or 21st century is known to have produced sovereignty.

Readers often point out that private buyers did get ruling rights in the past, and this is true. The Liechtenstein family paid 115,000 guilders for Schellenberg and 290,000 for Vaduz because it needed land directly under the emperor to earn a seat in the Imperial Diet. The emperor joined them into a principality in 1719, and it became sovereign in 1806 when Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine took it out of the empire. The Sultan of Brunei's representative granted James Brooke land in Sarawak in 1841, the sultan confirmed the appointment by July 1842, and the family ruled as Rajahs until 1946. The British North Borneo Company bought concessions from the Sultans of Brunei and Sulu in 1877 and 1878, issued laws and set up courts, and handed the territory to Britain in 1946. King Leopold II of Belgium held the Congo Free State as a personal possession from 1885 to 1908, a regime of forced labour and mass death that ended when an international campaign led Belgium to annex it. Each of these rested on an emperor, sultan, king or great power willing to agree, and on an age when empires gave such grants. The International Court of Justice's Western Sahara opinion of 1975 explains how the law saw deals of this kind. Agreements with local rulers were treated as derivative roots of title, meaning that the buyer's title came from the ruler who gave it up. The land was not treated as empty and free to take. The North Borneo Company still needed a British royal charter, and it sold out to Britain for £860,000 in 1946. The Hudson's Bay Company held Rupert's Land, about a third of present-day Canada, under a 1670 charter, granted Lord Selkirk 300,000 square kilometres of it in 1811, and sold it through the Crown for £300,000 in 1869, while sovereignty lay with the Crown throughout. The Knights of Malta bought four Caribbean islands in 1651 with the French king keeping the final right to rule, and sold them in 1665. Jacques du Parquet bought Martinique in 1650, and the king revoked such sales in 1664. The Duchess of Atholl sold the lordship of Man to the Crown for £70,000 in 1765, which took an Act of Parliament. Sark's fief was sold in 1852 with the Queen's permission.

That earlier era also shows who was left out. Many of these purchases were made from peoples who did not understand the terms or who were later told they had no right to sell. Adolf Lüderitz bought coastal land in what is now Namibia in 1883, describing its width in German miles of about 7.4 kilometres to a chief who understood the English mile of 1.6, and Germans called it the Mile Swindle. Lobengula signed the Rudd Concession in 1888 and spent the next years trying to disown it. In Johnson v. M'Intosh in 1823, the US Supreme Court ruled that private buyers could not get good title from the Piankeshaw, because only the government holding sovereignty could buy out Native occupants. In 1835 the Governor of New South Wales declared John Batman's deal with Aboriginal elders for 600,000 acres near today's Melbourne void against the Crown. Virginia and North Carolina cancelled Richard Henderson's purchase from the Cherokee and paid him in land grants.

Today the normal result of buying land is ordinary ownership, and sometimes a very long lease. The Clunies-Ross family owned the Cocos Islands under an 1886 Crown grant while Britain and then Australia ruled them, and Australia paid A$6.25 million for most of their property in 1978. Firestone took up to a million acres of Liberia for 99 years in 1926, and the Golden Triangle zone in Laos runs on a 99-year lease in Lao territory. Kiribati, an actual country, paid $8.6 million in 2014 for about 22 square kilometres of Fiji, and it holds the land as an ordinary owner under Fijian law. Larry Ellison bought 98 percent of Lānaʻi in 2012 for $300 million, and it remains part of Hawaii. The Robinson family keeps Niʻihau closed to most outsiders, and it is still counted within Kauaʻi County. Palmyra Atoll shows how strong private title can be and where it stops. The US government sued the Fullard-Leo family, claiming the atoll had never been private, and the family won at the Supreme Court in 1947, yet the atoll was under US sovereignty the whole time. Martin Coles Harman, owner of Lundy, issued his own coins in 1929 and was convicted, and the High Court upheld that in 1931 because Lundy was part of England.

Even plain ownership can meet resistance if the purchase is large or held by foreigners. Iceland's law bars big purchases by outsiders, and its minister refused Huang Nubo an exemption in 2011 for about 300 square kilometres. Douglas Tompkins's Pumalín Park in Chile ran from the Pacific to the Argentine border, and parliament debated whether he was undermining sovereignty. Madagascar's new leader cancelled Daewoo's 99-year farm deal in 2009 after the protests that helped bring down his predecessor. The Solomon Islands Attorney-General declared a provincial lease of Tulagi unlawful in 2019. Satoshi Island's token sale in Vanuatu collapsed in 2025 because of a breach of the land lease, and Vanuatu had already said that a token gave no right of residence.

Selling is itself a legal hazard for a founder. Gregor MacGregor sold land and bonds in a country called Poyais that did not exist, and at least 180 of the roughly 250 settlers who sailed there in 1822 and 1823 died. Selling shares in a future country can count as selling securities, as Lazarus Long's New Utopia found when the US Securities and Exchange Commission sued him in 1999 over a $350 million bond offering that had raised $24,000.

The workable version is modest. A person can buy an island or a ranch, pay the taxes, run it privately under the rules of the host country and write whatever charter they please for their own members. Reading these rules, it seems that if a government did give up land by treaty to a new government, the title would be strong and hard to undo, and a treaty handover would answer the usual objection to a new state. Since a treaty needs a state on each side, the seller would in effect first have to accept the buyer as a state, as Italy did for the Holy See in the Lateran Treaty of 1929. No private buyer has been offered this. That is why legal standing and the ability to hold such land rate highly in this route while the chance of it happening at all stays near one percent. No such deal is known, and a government would need a reason to give one that outweighs the anger seen in Egypt in 2016, when the announced transfer of Tiran and Sanafir to Saudi Arabia set off the largest protests against the government since 2014.
essays.leases-and-extraterritorial-spots:
People often imagine that an embassy, a foreign military base or an airport transit lounge is a little piece of another country, or of no country at all. The legal picture is different, and understanding it shows why these places offer so little to someone who wants a territory of their own. In almost every case the host country keeps final authority. Another country or body runs the place under a lease, a treaty or a diplomatic rule, and what that occupant can do depends on the words of the agreement.

A lease between countries works much like a lease on a flat. The owner stays the owner, the tenant gets the use of the place, and the document says how long and on what terms. Guantánamo Bay, a US naval base of 117 square kilometres in Cuba, has been held under a lease since 1903. Article III of that lease shows the idea exactly. The United States recognises "the continuance of the ultimate sovereignty of the Republic of Cuba", the final legal right to rule, while it exercises "complete jurisdiction and control" as long as it occupies the land. It began at $2,000 a year in gold and has been $4,085 a year since 1974. A 1934 treaty, in Article III, says the lease can end only if both sides agree or the United States leaves. The Cuban government that took power in 1959 says the base was imposed by force and is illegal, and it has cashed one rent cheque since then, which Fidel Castro said was deposited by mistake. The base still operates, and Cuba still objects. In Boumediene v. Bush in 2008, the US Supreme Court ruled that detainees held there have a constitutional right to challenge their detention in court, so even that base is not a place without law.

Leases can also be forced on a weaker country, and they can run out. In 1898, after China's defeat by Japan, Britain leased the New Territories of Hong Kong, including 235 islands, for 99 years with no rent. The treaty is often described as an unequal one, meaning it was forced on a weaker state. Because the lease would end on 30 June 1997, Britain and China negotiated in advance, and under their 1984 Joint Declaration all of Hong Kong passed to China. The Panama Canal Zone, 1,432 square kilometres, was granted to the United States in perpetuity, which means with no end date. It had its own governor, courts and police. Riots in 1958, 1959 and 1964 led to negotiations, and the zone was abolished in 1979. So a grant with no end date came to an end after about 76 years, by a new treaty.

In all these known cases, the party receiving a lease was a country or a country-like body. The nearest thing to a private group is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that has diplomatic relations with more than 110 countries and no land of its own. A treaty signed in 1998 gives it the upper part of Fort St Angelo in Malta for 99 years, with listed privileges and legal protections. Either side may give notice in the 50th or 75th year, with the end taking effect five years later. Malta keeps ownership, its flag flies beside the Order's, Maltese courts generally have jurisdiction, and the Order may not grant asylum there. The Order had nine centuries of history behind it and worldwide humanitarian work, and it still got a use arrangement in a fort. No new founder has come close to such a deal.

Embassies work on a different principle. Article 22 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations says embassy premises are inviolable and that the host country's officers may not enter without the consent of the head of the mission. That rule protects the work of diplomats, and it does not turn the building into foreign soil. Article 41 says people with diplomatic privileges must respect the host country's laws and that the premises must not be used in ways incompatible with the mission's functions. Julian Assange showed what the rule gives and what it leaves out. He entered Ecuador's embassy in London, a suite of rooms on the ground floor of a block of flats, on 19 June 2012, and Ecuador granted him asylum. Britain did not accept the asylum. International law gives the embassy's government less here than people suppose. In the Asylum case of 1950 between Colombia and Peru, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, said that sheltering someone in an embassy derogates from the sovereignty of the host country, found that Colombia could not settle the nature of the offence by its own decision, and found no proven regional custom that would let it do so. Britain and Ecuador were not parties to that case, and reading it, it seems to support Britain's refusal without deciding it. It suggested that it could use a 1987 British law to enter, then withdrew the suggestion, and police guarded the building at a reported cost of £6.5 million in the first two years. He could not leave without being arrested, and he stayed nearly seven years. In April 2019 Ecuador's president ended the asylum and invited police in, and they arrested him. He was held in Belmarsh prison until June 2024, when he pleaded guilty in the Northern Mariana Islands to one US count of conspiring to obtain and publish national defence information and his sentence of five years and two months was counted as served, so he was freed that day. His safety depended entirely on the wishes of the government that ran the building. A private person can be there only as that government's guest, and a change of president ended it.

Airports are the place of the greatest misunderstanding. Films and news stories talk of an international zone, as if travellers past passport control had left the country. These zones are fully under the legal power of the country where they sit, and local law applies inside them. A court has said so in plain words. In Amuur v. France in 1996, about asylum seekers held at Paris-Orly airport, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that "despite its name, the international zone does not have extraterritorial status", that French law applied to them, and that holding them there was a deprivation of liberty that breached the European Convention on Human Rights. Mehran Karimi Nasseri lived in Terminal 1 of Charles de Gaulle Airport near Paris from 1988 to 2006, about 18 years, and French law applied to him throughout. Belgium and France both offered him residency, and he refused to sign because the papers did not use his chosen name. He gained no status from staying, and he died at the same airport on 12 November 2022. Edward Snowden spent 39 days in the transit area of Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow in 2013 after the United States revoked his passport, and he left when Russia granted him asylum. A transit area is a place people get stuck when no country will take them, and being stuck there gives them no rights over it.

Some other arrangements look similar. The UN headquarters in New York and its offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi are areas where the UN has been given some authority by agreement, and most local and national law still applies in them. The United States has a special visa, the C-2, so that delegates can attend meetings. The Tomb of Suleyman Shah in northern Syria was made a Turkish concession by the Treaty of Ankara in 1921, and Turkey moved it in 1973 and again in 2015, the second time on its own and over Syria's objection.

Suppose a group tried to use this route. They would first have to find a government willing to sign a lease with them on terms that give more than an ordinary tenant has. If a government offered only a normal lease, the group would be a tenant under that country's law, paying rent and tax. If it offered privileges, those would come through that country's own law or a treaty, and private groups cannot sign treaties in the sense governments use. Any term could end by notice, by a court or by the next government. Banks, insurers and suppliers would look at who holds final authority and would deal with that country's rules. Staff and residents would keep their existing citizenship and tax duties, and children born there would take their nationality from the rules of real countries.

The most workable version is a plain commercial lease of land, or a service role under a body that already has status. Either one can run for a long time. Herm, in the Channel Islands, has had tenants since 1737, and its lease was extended in 2023 to 2069. Neither gives any authority. The odds here reflect that. A lease can hold fairly well in law and in practice, and Guantánamo has lasted since 1903, but the agreement that does so is between states. Embassies and airports have sheltered people for years, and no territory passed to any of them.
essays.combo-investment-treaty-shield:
Most special zones rest on a promise from a government, and governments change. An investment treaty is an agreement between two countries in which each promises fair treatment to investors from the other, and it often lets an investor take a dispute directly to arbitration. Arbitration is a private hearing before appointed judges. The best-known forum is the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, or ICSID, a World Bank body. The idea here is to add a treaty on top of a zone, so that a later government that cancels the zone must pay for doing so. This combines a host's carve-out with protection from outside the host's own courts.

Some of this is clear. A treaty award is about money, and it does not restore a zone or give anyone a right to rule. Using the forum also requires consent, which comes from a treaty or a contract, because ICSID membership alone gives no investor a right to sue. Enforcement has real force, since member countries agree to treat an award like a ruling of their own courts. A country that repeals a scheme investors relied on can lose. Romania adopted investment incentives for certain regions in 1999, and investors built a large food business relying on them. Romania repealed them as part of joining the European Union, and in 2013 a tribunal found a breach of the Romania and Sweden treaty and awarded about £70 million plus interest. The European Commission then ruled that paying the award would be illegal state aid. The European General Court annulled that ruling in 2019, and in 2020 the United Kingdom Supreme Court unanimously lifted a stay so that enforcement could proceed in England. The dispute went on in the EU courts after that, and one later ruling of the General Court is reported to have again treated the award as state aid.

The live test is Próspera. It is a private zone on the island of Roatán, set up under the Honduran law on Zones for Employment and Economic Development, or ZEDEs. In April 2022 Honduras repealed the law, and on 20 September 2024 its Supreme Court declared the laws unconstitutional from the start. The owners filed Honduras Próspera Inc. and others v. Honduras, ICSID case ARB/23/2, relying on CAFTA-DR, the trade treaty linking the United States with Central America, and on a legal stability agreement with the state. The first demand was $10.775 billion, later reported as reduced to about $1.63 billion. Honduras left ICSID in 2024 and rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026, and the case was still pending in October 2026.

The open questions here are the ones that matter. No tribunal has yet ruled in the Próspera case on whether a promise made under a law later held void from the start can found a treaty claim. The Honduran Supreme Court's ruling treats the zones as never lawful, and the investors rely on promises the state made to them. President Castro's government described ending the zones as recovering sovereignty, and critics and supporters disagree over whether a claim of this kind should exist at all. Paul Romer, an economist who first promoted charter cities, has said Próspera is not close to a model he would recommend. A second open case has appeared in Australia. Landbridge, a Chinese company that holds a 99-year lease of the Port of Darwin, filed a claim at ICSID on 24 April 2026, saying Australia's actions were discriminatory, after both main parties promised in 2025 to return the port to Australian ownership. How that ends is not known. Panama's Supreme Court ruled in January 2026 that the contracts for two canal ports held by a CK Hutchison company were unconstitutional, and the company brought an arbitration claim at the International Chamber of Commerce.

Follow the steps. An investor needs the nationality of a country with a treaty, so the founders' passports and the place where the company is registered begin to matter. Next the host must agree to a stability contract or already have a treaty in force. When a later government moves against the zone, the investor files, and hearings run for years while legal costs mount. During that time local courts and police keep their powers, because a tribunal cannot order officers off the land. Reading the awards, it seems that the treaty shifts the cost of cancelling onto the state and leaves the decision with the state. Banks and insurers can take comfort from a treaty only as far as they believe an award can be collected, and Micula shows collection can take more than a decade after a 2005 filing.

The Sulu heirs' case shows a nearby failure. Eight claimants won a $14.92 billion award against Malaysia on an 1878 contract, and French courts undid it because the arbitrator lacked power. That case turned on whether Malaysia had ever agreed to the arbitrator, so the terms of consent decide whether any of this protection exists.

The route does have potential as a financial deterrent against a poor host, and that deterrent may buy time and a negotiated outcome. The strongest version is a clear treaty between two states, a specific stability contract signed by the proper authority, and a project built so that local people want it to continue. Even that version produces money or a settlement, and the land remains the host's. It has never produced recognition of anything as a state.
essays.combo-leased-private-operator:
Governments sometimes lease a port or a zone to a foreign company for a very long time. Long terms like 99 years invite people to treat these places as outposts, and a founder might hope for the same. The idea combines a long lease with the purchase route and a carve-out, with a private operator in place of a foreign government. A comparison with the Panama Canal Zone shows the difference between running a port and governing land.

The modern cases are plainly commercial, and that much is settled. In October 2015 the Northern Territory government in Australia gave Landbridge, a privately held Chinese company, a 99-year lease of the Port of Darwin for A$506 million. In July 2017 Sri Lanka's ports authority signed a 99-year lease of Hambantota's port with China Merchants Port for $1.12 billion, through a joint company, with a 15,000-acre economic zone also provided for. Sources give the company's share as either 70 or 85 percent. Neither lease moved sovereignty. Australian and Sri Lankan law still apply. In Laos, the Hong Kong-registered company in the Golden Triangle has 99 years on 10,000 hectares and its own immigration checkpoint, and that is on Lao soil. These leases hand over the operating of a business and a place.

The Canal Zone was a different legal thing. By a convention proclaimed in 1904, the United States received use, occupation and control of a strip of 1,432 square kilometres in perpetuity, and it ran its own governor, police, courts and judges. Panama's grant came straight after the American government had helped it become independent. A private body has never held such powers in modern times. Even that grant ended, with the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977, the end of the zone on 1 October 1979 and of the canal's joint running on 31 December 1999. It had caused riots in 1958, 1959 and 1964. A perpetual text lasted 75 years.

Recent events show how a host can undo a long lease. Reviews in 2021 and 2023 found no grounds to cancel Darwin's lease. In April 2025 the Australian prime minister said the country wanted to buy it back, both main parties promised to return it, and in January 2026 China's ambassador warned against the plan. On 24 April 2026 Landbridge filed a claim at ICSID, saying Australia's actions were discriminatory. In Panama, Hutchison's company ran the Balboa and Cristobal ports from the 1990s, and its contract renewed for 25 years in 2021. The Supreme Court ruled the contracts unconstitutional on 29 January 2026, after a suit brought the year before during American pressure on Panama. Reports in February 2026 said the government ordered the ports occupied, and the company has since claimed losses of more than $2 billion in arbitration. In Solomon Islands, the Tulagi deal of 2019 died within weeks because a province had no power to make it.

What is open is first of all about motive. At Hambantota, critics called the lease a debt trap. The payment was mostly used to pay other debts, and scholars including Brautigam and Brown dispute that account, with Brown arguing that China took on more risk and got entangled in local politics. The second open question is how far an international tribunal can reach, as in Darwin. Neither has been resolved. Sri Lanka's foreign minister called the lease a mistake in 2021, and the deal stands.

Follow what a private founder would face. The founder needs serious money first, because these deals cost from hundreds of millions of dollars upward. Next is a bidding process, which is often public, and security reviews at home and in the host. A port needs an operating record, cranes and shipping lines, and insurers will want one. The operator would pay local tax, unless a special law exempts it, employ local people, and follow local customs law. Police and courts remain the host's. People on the land have no new nationality. A home-country government may also be pulled in. The Hutchison sale to a BlackRock-led consortium stalled over objections from the Chinese government, which shows that a company's home state can have a say as well.

The strongest version is what these operators do have. It is a well-capitalised company with a concession under clear law and a treaty behind it, and a host that keeps getting benefits. That gives a long period of operating control over valuable land, and often a say in what is built there. It is a useful commercial position. It is not, and has not been in any modern case, a path to ruling people or leaving the host's legal order. Reading the leases and the rulings, it seems that the longer and larger the lease, the more it draws political attention to its strategic importance.
essays.combo-company-special-district:
The idea is to stop trying to leave a country and to become, in law, a small piece of its local government. In the United States and many other places, a state legislature creates counties, cities and special districts, which are public bodies with narrow jobs such as water or roads. A company that owns nearly all the land in one spot can ask for such a body and then fill it with its own people. This combines a claim inside a state, a carve-out granted by a host, and the capture of a town. What comes out is real public power, including taxes, bonds, building codes and sometimes police, held by a private owner in practice.

The largest example is Walt Disney World. Disney bought land near Orlando through shell companies, and on 12 May 1967 Florida's governor signed the law creating the Reedy Creek Improvement District and two cities. The district ran land use, building codes, utilities, roads and fire protection. Votes went to landowners, one per acre, and Disney owned most of the land, so it effectively chose the board. The Florida Supreme Court held in 1968 that the law did not break the state constitution.

Some of this is settled law. American courts apply a rule that each voter counts equally in electing local government, and the United States Supreme Court made a narrow exception in Ball v. James in 1981. There it upheld voting by landowners, weighted by acres, for an Arizona water district, because the district's purpose was specialised and its burdens fell on landowners. It is equally settled that ownership of a town does not remove the rights of the people in it. In Marsh v. Alabama in 1946 a Jehovah's Witness was arrested for handing out leaflets in Chickasaw, a town owned by a shipbuilding company. The Court ruled for her and said that ownership does not always mean absolute dominion. And it is settled that a legislature can undo what it made. Florida voted in April 2022 to dissolve the district. In February 2023 it kept the district under a new name and gave the governor the power to appoint the five board members. Pullman, Illinois, ended the same way in an earlier age, when the state's highest court in 1898 ordered the company to sell all property not used for industry, and the company did not fully comply until 1907.

What remains open is narrower than the headlines. Nobody has settled how general a body can be and still keep landowner voting. Ball v. James stressed that the Arizona district was narrow, and Reedy Creek did far more than deliver water, but the 1968 Florida ruling and the 1981 federal case do not answer that for a full city with residents. Disney limited its residents to the two small cities partly from fear that a 1968 case, Avery v. Midland County, would force votes for all residents. The second open point was the agreement Disney and the old board signed just before the state took control, which limited the new board's power and used a clause running until 21 years after the death of the last living descendant of King Charles III. A federal judge ruled against Disney in January 2024 on its suit against the governor, Disney settled the state cases in March 2024, and no court finished deciding whether the agreement was valid.

Now follow the idea through. Suppose a company owns a large tract in a state with a friendly legislature. It first needs a bill, and bills draw neighbours. Blockchains, Inc. owned about 67,000 acres in Storey County, Nevada, and in 2021 wanted a new form of government there, called an Innovation Zone, for a planned 36,000 residents. The governor promoted it in his State of the State address, Storey County objected on money and logistics, critics called it a company town, questions arose about water, and the legislature sent it to a study committee. The company withdrew in October 2021 after saying it had spent more than $300 million in Nevada. A company that does get its district still has every ordinary tie to the state. Its staff are citizens, its bonds are sold under securities law, and federal law applies throughout. Reading the text of these cases, it seems that the power rests on continued political tolerance, and that the size of the project raises the price of removing it. Critics of the 2022 Florida law pointed to more than $1 billion in district bonds.

Small places show how far control can go through housing alone. Vernon, California, is an industrial city founded in 1905 where the city owned nearly all the homes and tenants were mostly city employees or linked to them. It had 112 people in 2010. In 2006 outsiders moved in to run for council, the city cut their power and tried to evict them, and a judge let them run, and they lost. State lawmakers nearly dissolved Vernon in 2011, and the Assembly voted 58 to 7 to do so, before the Senate rejected the bill after Vernon accepted reforms and agreed to set aside $60 million for nearby cities. Criminal charges had already reached its mayor and administrator. Starbase, Texas, is the newest case. Voters there approved a city in May 2025 under ordinary state rules, with a SpaceX vice-president unopposed as mayor. Outside the United States, the Hawksbill Creek Agreement of 1955 let Wallace Groves and the Grand Bahama Port Authority develop and administer Freeport, under terms extended to 2054. A tribunal in March 2026 rejected both the government's $357 million claim and most of the company's counterclaims, including the claim to exclusive authority over the area.

The strongest version is a large landowner with a single friendly legislature, a narrow stated purpose, broad public services and long-term bonds. That can last for generations, as Reedy Creek lasted 56 years and Freeport has lasted 71. It gives local power and no separation from the country. Taxes to the higher government, criminal law and the constitution all continue, and recognition by a foreign state is not part of what this route can produce.
essays.inside-state:
A micronation is a self-declared country, usually very small, that no government accepts as a country. The most common kind sits on land inside an existing state, such as a farm, a house, a village or a desert plot. Anyone can make such a declaration, and nothing stops it. Legally the land stays in the country whose borders surround it, and its courts go on applying its tax and criminal law to you as usual.

Founders often cite the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty. Article 1 asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other states, and Article 3 says a state's existence does not depend on recognition by others. The tests do not say in words that the land must be free of another state's claim, and disputed borders alone do not stop a place being a state. The difficulty inside a country lies with the government test. Lawyers read it to mean a government that actually controls the place and is independent of others, and the Supreme Court of Canada, in its Quebec reference of 1998, said a breakaway's success in fact would depend on effective control of a territory and on recognition by the international community. Reading those tests, a farm or a house where the surrounding country's police, courts and tax office go on working has neither, so the tests are not met. No micronation has ever become a state.

Sealand is a useful comparison. It is an old sea fort off Suffolk, declared independent in 1967. An English judge ruled in 1968 that a firearms law did not reach it, because Parliament had never extended that law beyond the three-mile limit. The fort had a real argument based on its location until Britain extended its waters to 12 miles in 1987. A farm in Australia never had that argument.

A declaration can still accomplish real things, and most of them involve attention. Protest is the first. In 1977 squatters on Freston Road in London, facing demolition, held a referendum, declared the Republic of Frestonia and applied to the United Nations. The press coverage made demolition harder, the council dropped it by 1982, and residents formed a housing co-operative that still manages homes on the site. Aramoana in New Zealand declared independence in 1980 to fight an aluminium smelter. The smelter was never built, after a partner company left. Rainbow Creek in Victoria seceded in 1979 over flooding, and the dispute was never resolved. The Principality of Wy in Sydney drew coverage in several countries in a fight over a driveway, lost its appeal in 2013, and never got the driveway.
