Tourism is the second use and the most reliable. Key West's Conch Republic began in 1982 as a protest against a federal roadblock and now runs a week-long festival each April. Laàs in France, a village of 135 people, sells day trips with a customs booth and received 28 buses in 2018. Seborga in Italy has sentry boxes and an elected prince, Užupis in Vilnius stamps visitors' passports each 1 April, and Whangamomona in New Zealand holds a Republic Day festival. Art and humour are the third use, as with Lars Vilks's Ladonia in Sweden, declared in 1996 over a council's order against his sculptures, and the joke republic of Molossia in Nevada.

Now follow what happens if someone means it seriously. The first letter usually comes from the tax office. Leonard Casley declared his 75-square-kilometre wheat farm the Hutt River Province in 1970, after a quota let him sell only about 40 of his 4,000 hectares of crop. He issued passports, coins and stamps, drew a reported 40,000 tourists a year, and claimed about 14,000 citizens with 23 residents. He was prosecuted in 1977 for failing to give the Taxation Office documents. In June 2017 Justice Le Miere of the Supreme Court of Western Australia ordered him to pay more than A$2.7 million and his son more than A$242,000, saying the sovereignty argument "has no legal merit or substance". The judge added that anyone can declare themselves a sovereign in their own home "but they cannot ignore the laws of Australia or not pay tax". The principality was dissolved in August 2020, and the farm went on sale. Molossia's Kevin Baugh and Zaqistan's Zaq Landsberg took another course. They pay county property tax and call it foreign aid and tributes, and their counties have no dispute with them. In the United States, claiming not to be a citizen for income tax purposes has brought criminal and civil penalties, and a return based on a position the tax agency lists as frivolous can bring a $5,000 penalty.

The courts come next, and a pattern appears. Stuart Hill, who declared the islet of Forvik in Shetland in 2008, was charged in 2011 with motoring offences on vans he called consular vehicles. He gave Lerwick Sheriff Court a 71-page argument that it had no power in Shetland. The sheriff heard it over two days, called him deluded and seriously misguided, and dismissed it. He was fined £1,400, and in December 2025 another sheriff rejected the same argument. Around 2006 Casley lost again to the tax office, and the High Court of Australia dismissed his application as fatuous, frivolous and vexatious, a phrase for a case with no legal merit. A court draws its power from the state that created it, so it does not treat a litigant's own declaration as a limit on that power.

Micronation founders share this ground with sovereign citizens and "freemen on the land", people who argue that the law applies to them only if they consent. In Meads v. Meads in 2012, a judge in Alberta, Canada, reviewed these arguments in detail and wrote that a decade of cases had failed to prove a single one of their concepts. No recorded case has upheld them. Trying them can make things worse. British courts have jailed such litigants for contempt or for unpaid council tax, and a Queensland court dismissed an appeal in 2020 from a man fined A$150 for driving unlicensed who said he was outside Queensland law.

Police usually arrive over cars or guns. Queensland police charged a Yidindji minister in 2015 over his own government's licence and plates. Alec Brackstone of Bumbunga claimed diplomatic immunity on a firearms charge in 1999, and the claim failed. George Muirhead declared two Queensland properties independent in 1993 to stop repossession, and police evicted him eleven days later. Force turns this into serious crime. Republic of Texas members kidnapped a couple in 1997, and their leader went to prison with a projected release date of 2041. Salvatore Meloni, who seized a private island off Sardinia in 2008, was convicted in 2012 of illegally occupying land and of environmental damage and got 20 months. Jailed in April 2017 on tax offences, he died in custody that July after a two-month hunger strike.

Money and papers cause the next problems. A declaration does not change a mortgage. The Jensen family of Snake Hill told a court in 2011 that the Bank of Queensland's foreclosure was a matter for international law, and a judge dismissed the claim. John Rudge of Avram is an unusual case. His unlicensed bank's reserves were seized, and after six cases costing about A$22 million the courts found nothing illegal and ordered them returned. Passports have done the most harm. Edwin Lipburger of Kugelmugel was sentenced to 10 weeks in Austria in 1979 for unlawful assumption of public authority. A man was arrested in Germany for trying to use a Hutt River diplomatic passport, and the Council of the European Union listed such passports as fantasy documents. Malaysia detained the daughters of the Sunda Empire's founders in 2007 for entering on its diplomatic passports. Planning law is another trap. Kugelmugel began as a house built without a permit, and a court ordered Ladonia's third sculpture removed in 1999.

Tolerance lasts as long as a project costs the government little. Their activities are usually too trivial to dispute. Hutt River's local shire listed it as having historic significance, and a state minister called its prince an enigma, while Australian diplomats exchanged 120 cables about it from 1984 to 2010. Occupying land the state wants goes differently. Alcatraz's occupiers were removed after 19 months, the Free Republic of Wendland after 33 days, and Seattle's protest zone after 23 days and two deaths. About a thousand Nigerian soldiers attacked Fela Kuti's Kalakuta compound in 1977, and it burned down.

Long survival usually needs numbers, land or a deal. Christiania in Copenhagen outlasted a 1978 Supreme Court clearance order, and residents bought part of its land in 2012. It is now under ordinary Danish law. The ZAD near Nantes stopped an airport, and many of its projects moved into ordinary French land law. Orania in South Africa bought its town and has generally been left alone. The Zapatistas have governed communities in Chiapas since a 1994 uprising, and in 2023, after increased cartel violence, they announced that they were dissolving their autonomous municipalities and replacing them with smaller local autonomous governments. Indigenous claims such as the Murrawarri Republic and the Republic of Lakotah raise deeper arguments about land never given up. The Australian government has not acknowledged the first, and recognised tribal governments did not back the second.

The workable version is honest about what it is. Own your land, pay your taxes, follow planning rules, keep your real passport, register an association as Flandrensis and Laàs did, and label your papers as souvenirs. That can produce a good story, a festival, a campaign tool or a business. It can last for years if the state finds it harmless. It has little legal force and almost no prospect of recognition, because no state has a reason to accept part of another state on the strength of a declaration.
essays.territorial-sea:
The territorial sea is the belt of water next to a coast. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, a country may set it at up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 km) from its baselines, the lines from which sea zones are measured (Article 3). The normal baseline is the low-water line on the country's official charts (Article 5).

Inside this belt the coastal country has full authority over the water, the seabed under it and the air above it, the same as over its land (Article 2). The main limit is innocent passage, the right of foreign ships to pass through peacefully and without delay (Articles 17 to 19). A private road that the owner must let travellers use is similar, since a traveller may drive through and may not stop and build a house. Passage has to be continuous, and stopping is allowed only for ordinary navigation, emergencies or helping people in danger (Article 18), so settling in one spot falls outside it.

A further belt, the contiguous zone, can reach out to 24 nautical miles if the country declares one. There the country may act to prevent or punish customs, tax, immigration and health offences committed in its territory or territorial sea (Article 33).

The practical result is that a structure here is a domestic building project. Suppose a group anchors a platform 5 nautical miles off a coast and declares independence. The group is inside the country, in the same legal position as someone who puts up an unapproved building on land and announces that it is a new state. Harbour, building, tax and police officials all have ordinary powers. A nearby officer can visit, and the group's boats have to land at that country's docks.

Giorgio Rosa's Rose Island shows how little room there is even near the line. His 400-square-metre platform stood nearly 12 km off Rimini, a few hundred metres outside Italian waters as they were then measured. The Rimini harbour office asked him to stop in late 1966. He declared independence on 1 May 1968, and police and tax officers took control on 26 June, about eight weeks later. A project inside the limit would not even have the argument about position that Rosa made.

The line itself is less simple than it looks, and two British cases teach this. Roy Bates ran a pirate radio station on Knock John, a wartime fort about 16 km off Essex, where British broadcasting law could reach him only if the fort lay inside the three-mile limit then used. Distance is measured from a line set by law, which need not follow the shore. Magistrates fined him £100 in 1966, and his appeal failed when the court held that the fort lay on the landward side of that line. Radio 390, on Red Sands fort, lost in the High Court in December 1966, two judges to one, because the distance could be measured from a sandbank that shows only at low water. UNCLOS keeps the same idea today. Land that shows only at low tide can serve as a baseline if it lies within the territorial sea's width of the coast (Article 13). Neither fort had moved. A person therefore cannot judge the limit with a map and a ruler from the beach.

A country can also move the line. Bates went on to Roughs Tower, which he declared to be Sealand in 1967. The fort sits about 6 to 7 nautical miles off the English coast, or about 11 to 13 km, and at that time it was outside British waters. A British court said so in 1968, when it held that it could not try his son on firearms charges there. In 1987 the UK extended its territorial waters to 12 nautical miles, which put the fort in waters recognized as British. Offshore installations and artificial islands, for their part, do not count as harbour works and cannot push the boundary out in the builder's favour (Article 11). So the limit can grow toward a project, and a project cannot grow the limit.

Three real projects show what is possible when the country's law is accepted from the start. The Seasteading Institute of San Francisco chose French Polynesia, a self-governing French territory, for its calm lagoons. In January 2017 the territory's government signed a memorandum of understanding with the institute, a document that records intentions and is usually weaker than a contract. It opened the way to studies of "seazones" with a special governing framework, and the institute formed a company, Blue Frontiers. Residents objected and opposition politician Valentina Cross protested. On 28 February 2018 it was reported that the government considered the deal to have no legal force and to have expired at the end of 2017. Nothing was built. The memorandum had bound the government to very little, so it could simply let the plan lapse.

SeaPods came from Ocean Builders, the same company whose cabin off Phuket was raided by the Thai navy in 2019. It turned to homes at Linton Bay Marina in Panama, with $100 deposits and prices from about $295,000 to $1.5 million. Each home stands above the water on a float tethered to the seabed by anchors. At the unveiling on 22 September 2022, in front of an audience that included Panama's president, the prototype tipped over with people inside. The company blamed a failed bilge pump, the pump that clears water from a hull, and denied that it sank, and no injuries were reported. Guests were staying in one by June 2023. The company claims no independence, and the number of permanent residents is not known.

Oceanix Busan is the largest of the three. On 18 November 2021 the city of Busan in South Korea, UN-Habitat and the company OCEANIX agreed to build a prototype floating district, with about $200 million anticipated as the cost, and they unveiled the design at UN Headquarters in April 2022. At the developers' later figure of $10,000 per square metre, its 15.5 acres would come to about $627 million. A conference in October 2023 gave no concrete financing or construction plans, construction is not known to have started, and no one is known to live there. This project attempts to build on the sea while staying fully inside South Korean law.

The ordinary bumps follow from being inside a country. Permits come first, and residents can stop them, as in French Polynesia. Ocean Builders' cruise ship plan outside national waters collapsed in 2020 when no insurer would give liability cover, which shows how much depends on insurance anywhere at sea. Tax on residents stays as it was. The US taxes citizens on worldwide income, and the host country may tax local income too. Medical care, schooling, inheritance and birth records run through the country's normal systems, which is an advantage for families. Police and courts have the same reach as on the shore, so a dispute over a floating home would go to an ordinary local court.

The common misunderstandings come from treating water as different from land. A boat's flag does not take a settled home out of the coastal country's law, since passage rights do not cover staying. A declaration does not change the zone either. Stuart Hill, who declared a Shetland islet the state of Forvik in 2008, was still charged with motoring offences in a Scottish court. Recognition is as far away as it is anywhere else, since UN membership needs nine of 15 Security Council votes with no veto and two-thirds of the General Assembly.

The most workable version is a licensed floating neighbourhood or marina, or at most a special zone written into the host country's law by its legislature. Calm water, short supply lines and a nearby hospital make building here among the easier options at sea, and holding out against the coastal country close to impossible. Any self-government lasts only as long as that country's politics allow, and a memorandum alone gives no protection.
essays.abandoned-platforms:
Steel and concrete structures stand in open water off many coasts, and some are no longer in use. A disused platform already has a deck and legs and needs no dredging, so people have tried since the 1960s to use wartime sea forts and purpose-built platforms as bases for independent projects.

The first thing to understand is that an empty structure is not an ownerless one. Two separate kinds of right apply. One is ownership, which belongs to whichever company or government built or bought it, and entering without permission can be trespass. The other is legal power over the place, which belongs to a country. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, an installation in a country's exclusive economic zone, the belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles from its coast where it controls resources, stays under that country's sole legal power. The same applies on its continental shelf, the seabed extending out from the coast (Articles 60 and 80). Oil platforms stand on a shelf, so they normally fall under that power. Buying a platform from its owner would appear to transfer ownership only, because the country's legal power does not come with the sale.

The treaty also expects old structures to disappear. Abandoned or disused installations must be removed to keep shipping safe, and any part left standing must be made public so that ships can avoid it (Article 60(3)). In practice that duty usually reaches the operator through the coastal country's own rules. Sinking one is no easy way out, since the London Protocol, a treaty on dumping, treats all dumping at sea as prohibited unless explicitly permitted. A platform has no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has, so it cannot be the base of a claim to the water around it (Article 60(8)). Nor is it part of the coast when boundaries are drawn (Article 11).

Suppose a group boards a disused oil platform 50 miles off a coast and raises a flag. Boarding is physically possible. The owner, who may still be responsible for removing the platform, now has unauthorized people on its property. The coastal country has legal power over the structure, so its police or navy can come out. If anyone is hurt, or the structure fails, the questions of who pays would go to that country's courts.

Sealand is the case everyone cites. Roughs Tower was built by Britain in 1943 and sunk in place on a sandbar, about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk and 7 off Essex. That was then outside Britain's three-mile territorial sea. Roy Bates, a former army major, had just lost a court case over Radio Essex on Knock John, another fort, because the court found that fort lay on the landward side of the legal line measuring the limit. He moved to Roughs Tower, took it from Radio Caroline staff, and declared the Principality of Sealand on 2 September 1967. In May 1968 his son Michael fired a pistol near a boat servicing a buoy. A judge at Chelmsford ruled that October that the firearms law did not apply, because Parliament had never extended it beyond three miles. That ruling decided only how far a statute reached. In 1978 a Cologne court held that Sealand was no state, in a case brought by Alexander Achenbach, a German who had drafted its constitution. That August Achenbach's associates seized the fort while the elder Bateses were away, and the family retook it by helicopter. In 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which now covers the tower, and it has left the place alone since. The Bates family says Britain and Germany have recognized it in practice, and neither government accepts this. Roy Bates died in 2012. Michael lives in England, the family sells titles and an online citizenship at about $10 a month, and one caretaker lives on the fort. Sealand's fort stood outside the limit when the claim began, and a new project would not have that history.

Other governments did not leave their forts alone. Sunk Head, about 18 km off Essex, stood clearly outside British waters too. When the law banning offshore broadcasting took effect in August 1967, Royal Engineers placed 3,200 pounds of explosives and blew it up on 21 August, leaving only stumps. Red Sands, home of Radio 390, lost in the High Court in 1966 on a measurement from a sandbank that shows only at low water, and it went off the air on 14 August 1967 under the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act. In June 1966 men boarded Radio City's fort in a dispute over a transmitter, its owner Reginald Calvert was shot dead at the home of a rival, Oliver Smedley, and Smedley was cleared on grounds of self-defence. The killing turned public feeling against the stations, and enforcement rose.

REM Island was built for commercial radio and television about 10 km off Noordwijk and fixed to the seabed in cement, beyond Dutch territorial waters as then measured. Broadcasts began in August 1964. The Dutch Senate passed a law on 1 December 1964, and the government put it into effect on 12 December. Accounts differ on whether it declared the seabed below the platform Dutch territory or applied Dutch law to installations on the Dutch part of the continental shelf. Boats and police helicopters arrived five days later, and accounts differ on whether marines or police officers boarded. Rose Island, a 400-square-metre platform nearly 12 km off Rimini, declared independence on 1 May 1968. Italian police and tax officers took control on 26 June, about eight weeks later, and blockaded it. The navy set explosive charges twice in February 1969, the second time on 13 February, and a storm sank what remained on 26 February. The Council of State, Italy's top administrative court, held the independence claims unfounded and said Italian citizens stay subject to Italian law abroad.

Holding a fort leaves the other problems open. HavenCo was set up on Sealand in 2000 to keep customers' data beyond the reach of courts. Law professor James Grimmelmann found that the dot-com crash cut Sealand's internet links more than any government did. Co-founder Ryan Lackey left in 2002 after disputes with the Bates family and could not sue, because Sealand's monarch headed its courts and going to a foreign court would have undercut the claim of independence. Operations stopped in 2008. Banks need a supervisor they can rely on, and a fort has none. Sealand's passports were revoked in 1997 after a Madrid-based ring sold fakes, and using such a document at a border may bring charges. Unauthorized broadcasting from the high seas can be prosecuted by several countries, including any country that receives the signal, and their ships may arrest those involved (Article 109). Old steel and concrete need upkeep, and a 2006 fire on Sealand sent one person to hospital, with damage estimates ranging from £100,000 to half a million pounds. People on board keep their home countries' tax duties, and a rescue lands them in another country. Locking someone up on the platform could also be treated as unlawful detention by another country's courts, since no one else accepts the platform's own courts.

Common misunderstandings follow from Sealand's fame. The 1968 British ruling said a statute stopped at three miles and did not recognize Sealand. Occupying a structure gives no title to it, and buying one gives no country. The usual test for a state, in the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with others. Sealand has had one or two residents in recent years, and its territory is a deck that UNCLOS treats as no island.

The most workable version is an ordinary lease or purchase from the owner, with the coastal country's approval, for a business such as research or tourism, under that country's law and with a plan for eventual removal. REM Island's later life points the same way. The Dutch government used it to measure sea temperature and salt levels, and it has been a restaurant in Amsterdam's harbour since 2011. A new occupation claiming independence would have little legal basis on a shelf or in an exclusive economic zone, and most of its chance of lasting would depend on a government choosing not to act.
essays.ships-flag:
People live on ships today, for years at a time, and nobody sends a warship to stop them. To see what that does and does not give a person, it helps to understand the flag.

Every ship on the high seas, the open ocean outside any country's control, belongs to a country in legal terms. The flag state is the country whose flag the ship flies and whose register lists it. The system comes from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Nobody owns the open sea, so without some link to a country no law would reach what happens on a ship there. Under Article 90 every country, including one with no coast, may sail ships under its flag. Under Article 91 each country sets its own conditions for its flag, and there must be a "genuine link" between the country and the ship. Under Article 92(1) a ship may fly one flag only, and on the high seas only the flag state has legal power over it, except in cases set by treaty or by UNCLOS. Article 92(2) says a ship using two or more flags as it suits may be treated as having no nationality.

The register works a little like a passport for the vessel, with duties attached. Article 94 requires the flag state to keep a register and enforce rules on seaworthiness, crew and safety. Article 97 says that after a collision, only the flag state or the person's own country may bring criminal charges. Article 98 says each flag state must require captains to rescue people in danger at sea. Article 99 says any slave who reaches any ship, under any flag, is free by that fact. Open registers accept foreign-owned ships for a fee, which is why The World flies the flag of the Bahamas although it is managed from Florida. Each register sets its own limits. Liberia, for example, asks for a waiver and a willing inspection body for vessels over 20 years old.

A flag issued by a place no other country recognizes gives no protection. Article 110 lets a warship board a foreign ship if it has reasonable grounds to suspect piracy, slave trading, unauthorized broadcasting (where its own country has power under Article 109), that the ship has no nationality, or that a ship flying a foreign flag or refusing to show one really has the warship's nationality. The ground that matters for self-declared flags is Article 110(1)(d), having no nationality. The treaty does not mention unrecognized flags, but a court has dealt with the point. In Naim Molvan v Attorney General for Palestine, decided on 20 April 1948, the Privy Council, the British Empire's top court of appeal, considered the Asya, a ship stopped on 27 March 1946. It flew no flag, then a Turkish flag it could not show it was entitled to, then a Zionist flag. Lord Simonds wrote that freedom of the open sea is "freedom of ships which fly and are entitled to fly the flag of a State which is within the comity of nations". The Zionist flag was not the flag of any state in being, so no state could claim protection for the ship, and the court held that seizing it breached no international law. That is one British ruling from before UNCLOS. Article 110 itself speaks of boarding and checking, and how much further a warship may go against such a ship is not spelled out there. US law, for one, calls a vessel "without nationality" in several situations, including when the country named denies the registry, and applies its drug law to such vessels (46 USC 70502). Full protection from boarding by other countries applies only to warships and government ships not used for trade, under Articles 95 and 96.

Registering is the easy route. Suppose a group buys a used cruise ship and registers it. They live under that country's law on board, and it can remove them from its register. A ship can only be sovereign in the legal sense if a country stands behind it, which brings the project back to the need for recognition by other countries. The first test comes from insurers, as MS Satoshi shows. Ocean Builders bought a 1991 cruise ship in 2020 to anchor in the Gulf of Panama. Protection and indemnity insurance, the liability cover owners need against claims at sea, was not available. The company said the closest offer was a $1 million premium for $5 million of cover. It asked Panama to class the ship as non-seagoing, which would have removed about 32 of 35 treaties, and Panama refused because it had an engine and a flag. Without insurance there could be no crew, which meant losing class, the safety rating from an inspection body, and then the flag. The ship was sold for scrap on 18 December 2020, but it was not broken up. It stayed at Panama until March 2021, when a British Virgin Islands company bought it for a cruise start-up, and Ambassador Cruise Line put it back into service in 2022 as the Ambience.

Maintenance and money come next. Villa Vie Odyssey was a 30-year-old ship sold as a home, with cabins from $99,999 plus monthly fees. It sat for months in a Belfast yard before sailing on 30 September 2024. On 26 October 2026 at Sihanoukville in Cambodia, residents were told to leave because the company could not secure fuel, and more than 200 went ashore. The chief executive said the company planned to file for Chapter 11, the US bankruptcy process, and no filing had been reported by 29 October. Residents held a contract with a company, so their home depended on that company's money. Life at Sea Cruises sold a three-year voyage with no ship and cancelled in November 2023. By January 2024 only four passengers had refunds, and 78 customers asked US prosecutors to investigate about $16 million in deposits. How that ended is not known. Blueseed, a startup ship planned off California to avoid work visas, never raised the $18 million it needed. Freedom Ship, a plan for 80,000 people, has seen its estimate rise from $6 billion to as much as $20 billion, and Pangeos, at $8 billion, remains a design. MS The World is the working model. It was completed in 2002 and has 165 residences owned by residents, who elect an advisory board.

Women on Waves, a Dutch group, takes women to international waters to give abortion pills under the law of its Dutch flag and a Dutch permit. Portuguese warships blocked it in 2004, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled in February 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression. Guatemala's army blocked the pier within 24 hours of docking. A flag gives no right to enter a port.

Coastal states have also learned to reach ships through the shore. Radio Mercur broadcast to Denmark until a 1962 law banned supporting it. Radio Nord flew Nicaragua's flag until Sweden pressed Nicaragua, and moved to Panama, and then Sweden banned selling its advertising. It closed in 1962. Radio Veronica and Radio North Sea International, whose ship Mebo II was firebombed in 1971, closed under a Dutch law of 1974. Radio Caroline kept going from international waters after Britain's 1967 Act made it illegal for British subjects to supply or advertise on it, until fuel and supplies ran out in 1990. The gambling ship SS Rex, off Santa Monica, won an appeal over how to measure a bay, and in 1939 California's Attorney General, Earl Warren, raided it as a public nuisance. On 20 November 1939, in People v. Stralla, the California Supreme Court held that Santa Monica Bay is a bay inside the state's boundary, measured from a line between Point Vicente and Point Dume, so the Rex had been anchored within state jurisdiction. It upheld the conviction of Harold Adams on that ground. The broadcasting laws left the ships alone and went after the people on land who supplied them and sold their advertising. Sea Shepherd adds another warning. In 2013 a US appeals court called its attacks on whalers piracy, holding that "private ends" means more than money, and piracy opens a ship to any warship regardless of flag. The court later held the group in contempt, it agreed in 2015 to pay $2.55 million, and a settlement announced on 23 August 2016 permanently barred it and its founder Paul Watson from attacking the whalers or coming within 500 yards of their ships on the open sea.

The United States still taxes its citizens wherever they live under Cook v. Tait, and banks report accounts. A resident arriving in port falls under that port's law, and specialist medical care means going ashore. A child born at sea normally takes nationality from the parents. The 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, which 82 countries had joined as of January 2025, treats the birth as happening in the flag country only if the child would otherwise be stateless.

A common misunderstanding is that a flag creates a country. A flag gives a ship a nationality, and a government can withdraw it, which is why Swedish pressure on Nicaragua pushed Radio Nord's owners to Panama. Another is that a registered ship is lawless at sea, when the flag state's law applies. The workable version is an ordinary registered ship run by a solid company, with a private ownership agreement, as The World has. Living there is estimated as very achievable, while recognition as a state is estimated at close to nothing, because residents trade independence for stability.
essays.combo-always-moving-habitat:
This idea avoids building anything fixed. A community lives on a ship that never stays long in one place, sailing across open ocean, passing through countries' coastal waters and calling at one port after another. It combines a flagged ship with the rule that lets ships pass through a country's waters, called innocent passage. The hope is that a home in constant motion never settles under any coastal government for long enough to be governed by it.

Much of this is settled and in the founder's favour. A ship under a real flag is lawful, and Article 90 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, gives every state the right to sail ships on the high seas. There, under Article 92, the ship answers only to its flag state. No treaty limits how long a ship may keep sailing. A moving ship also avoids the main rule that stops platforms. Article 60 gives a coastal state control over artificial islands and structures in its 200-mile resource zone, and a ship passing through is not one of these. Article 58 keeps the freedom of navigation in that zone for all countries. MS The World has worked this way since 2002, with residents who own their apartments and elect an advisory board, under the Bahamian flag.

The rules become tighter near a coast. The territorial sea is the belt up to 12 nautical miles from shore, where a country has full authority apart from the right of innocent passage (Article 17). Passage has a specific meaning. Article 18 says it means sailing through without entering port, or going to or from a port, and that it "shall be continuous and expeditious". Stopping and anchoring count only when they are a normal part of navigation or forced by distress. Article 19 lists what makes passage not innocent, including loading or unloading any person or goods contrary to customs or immigration laws, research, launching aircraft, and "any other activity not having a direct bearing on passage". So innocent passage is a right to cross. It is no basis for lingering, and it gives no right to live offshore in one spot within 12 miles.

Ports are the part most often misunderstood. A flag gives no right to enter a port. Ports lie in internal waters, and Article 25(2) recognises that a coastal state may set conditions on admission and act to prevent any breach of them. Women on Waves, whose Dutch-flagged ship carries a clinic, found this in 2004 when Portuguese warships blocked it. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression, but that ruling rested on human rights law. In Guatemala the army blocked the pier within 24 hours of the ship docking. Once in port, residents and the ship fall under that country's law as well.

Some points are open. Women on Waves also raises the unresolved question of whether a ship that docks, boards a country's citizens and takes them out for an act banned at home is passing innocently. Whether a ship used as a permanent home, returning to the same waters again and again, stays within the words "continuous and expeditious" has not been tested in any known ruling. Reading the text, it seems that the passage rules look at what the ship is doing on each trip through the belt, and that a home on a real route would be treated like any passenger ship. A ship that repeatedly drifted just offshore for residents' convenience would look more like the stopping that Article 18 does not allow. A practical point follows from this. A ship registered as seagoing has to keep the certificates and crew that go with that, and a resident community may struggle to pay for them.

Follow one year of such a life. The flag state's law applies on board. Crew and safety rules follow the flag, under Article 94. Every landing is an immigration event. A resident has to hold a passport and any visa that each port demands, so a person without valid papers stays on board or is refused. Food, fuel and spare parts come from ports, and repairs from shipyards. The move-along approach gives no escape from tax, because a citizen's home country may tax regardless of where the person sleeps, as the United States does under Cook v. Tait. Banks ask for a home address and a tax residence. Medical care beyond the ship's clinic means going ashore. A child born on board usually takes nationality from the parents, and the 1961 statelessness treaty treats the birth as occurring in the flag country only to prevent statelessness.

The cases show that the money usually fails before the law does. Villa Vie Odyssey sold cabins from $99,999, and on 26 October 2026 in Sihanoukville residents were told to leave because the company could not secure fuel. Life at Sea Cruises cancelled its three-year voyage in 2023 without ever having a ship. MS Satoshi failed for a different reason, because it was meant to stay at anchor, and liability insurers would not cover a ship used that way. That suggests that continual sailing can be easier to insure than sitting still, though the cost of fuel and crew is far higher.

This route has more practical potential than nearly any other at sea, and it achieves less in sovereignty. The strongest version is a solid company or residents' association owning a well-maintained ship under a respected flag, on a real itinerary, with a private contract setting the internal rules. Such a community can last for decades and choose where it goes. Its members stay citizens of their own countries, its flag state can remove it from the register, and any port can refuse it. Having no territory also leaves it without a basis for statehood under the usual tests.
essays.deep-seabed-area:
Beyond the continental shelves, the seabed that extends out from each country's coast, lies the deep ocean floor. By the International Seabed Authority's own figure, this area covers about 54% of the total area of the world's oceans. In law it is called "the Area". Nobody can own it.

The reason goes back to minerals. By the 1970s companies were preparing to collect manganese nodules, potato-sized lumps of metal on the deep floor, and no treaty said who could mine there. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the 1982 treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, answered by declaring the Area and its resources the "common heritage of mankind" (Article 136), meaning they belong to humanity as a whole. A shared fund run by one body for all its members works in a similar way, since no member may take a slice for itself.

Article 137 sets out the core rule. No country may claim authority over any part of the Area, no country or person may take any part of it as their own, and no such claim or taking will be recognized. Rights in the resources belong to humanity as a whole, and minerals can be sold only under the rules of the International Seabed Authority (ISA), based in Jamaica (Article 137(2)-(3)). The ISA is the body through which member countries control activities in the Area, and all UNCLOS members belong to it (Articles 156 and 157). It was set up on 16 November 1994. It had 172 members as of 6 February 2026, made up of 171 countries plus the European Union.

Other rules fill in the picture. The status of the water and air above stays the same (Article 135), so the water remains high seas, open ocean outside any country's control. The Area is open to use for peaceful purposes only (Article 141). Archaeological and historical objects found there are to be preserved or disposed of for the benefit of humanity (Article 149). Installations used for mineral activities must be placed and removed under ISA rules, and they "do not possess the status of islands", so they cannot have a territorial sea, a belt of coastal water (Article 147(2)).

To mine, an operator needs sponsorship from a member country and an approved plan of work (Article 153). A sponsor is a country that takes responsibility for the operator. This requirement closes the obvious route for a new state, since a self-declared country cannot sponsor itself. It is not a member, so it would have to find a real one willing to answer for it, and that puts the operation under that country's supervision.

Suppose a group sent down a submersible, placed a marker on the sea floor and announced a new country on it. A submersible visit needs no ISA permission if it is only a visit, because the ISA's control concerns mineral activities. The marker gives no title. Article 137 says the claim will not be recognized, so the group would hold a piece of equipment on the sea floor with no legal right to exclude others. If the group then started collecting nodules, it would be taking something that belongs to humanity as a whole, and anyone buying the metal would be dealing outside the ISA's rules.

Deepsea Ventures tried a careful version in 1974, before the treaty existed. This American company, of Gloucester Point, Virginia, wanted the nodules in a deposit of 60,000 square kilometres in the northeastern Pacific. On 15 November its president, John Flipse, sent a notice of discovery to Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, asked for diplomatic protection, and recorded a copy at a local courthouse. It claimed exclusive rights to mine and sell, and it said it was claiming no territory. It promised production within 15 years. The 1982 treaty later put the area under the authority, mining is not known to have taken place under the claim, and no court is known to have ruled on it.

Today the working system is contracts. The ISA lists 15-year exploration contracts with 22 contractors. Its text counts 19 for nodules, 7 for sulphides and 5 for crusts, 31 in all, although its sulphide sub-count adds up to 8, so the page is not fully consistent. Most are in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico. Only exploration is allowed so far. The rules for exploitation, meaning commercial mining, known as the Mining Code, were still unfinished after the July 2026 session of the ISA Council. The March 2026 Council approved no commercial mining, with benefit-sharing, liability and environmental compensation unresolved. In July the Council asked its staff for a roadmap and a new negotiating text, and the draft decision says commercial mining should not take place without rules.

The Metals Company shows the main challenge to this system. It began as DeepGreen Metals in 2011, and its subsidiaries hold ISA exploration contracts, NORI sponsored by Nauru and TOML sponsored by Tonga. In June 2021 Nauru told the ISA it meant to begin mining, which started a two-year deadline to finish the rules, and the rules were not finished. The US has not joined the UNCLOS deep-sea mining system. It has a rival route, the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980. On 24 April 2025 President Trump signed an order telling the US agency NOAA to speed up permits under that law, and within days the company's American arm applied. On 28 April 2026 NOAA found that the application met the law's information requirements, and on 19 August 2026 it published the company's consolidated application for an exploration licence and a commercial recovery permit. NOAA held a virtual public hearing on 13 October, and comments closed on 19 October with 1,663 received. Its page, last updated on 16 October 2026, listed no commercial recovery permit as issued. A separate exploration application was certified on 26 May 2026, and in August NOAA announced that it would prepare an environmental impact statement for it. The ISA's commission is investigating whether this breaches contractors' duties. On 18 July 2026 a specialist chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal ordered the ISA to respect fair procedure in the inquiry, without suspending it. Two days later the Council extended NORI's contract to 2031, and TOML's runs to January 2027 with an extension pending. The main case is undecided. If this route succeeds, it would give mining rights under one country's law and no territory to anyone.

Ordinary diving cannot reach these depths, so every visit needs a specialised vessel and submersible, and the seafloor elsewhere reaches more than 8 km. Food, power and rescue would all come from the surface, and rescue ends in some other country's port. Nothing built here would have island status. Any investor offered shares in a seabed nation would be buying a claim that Article 137 says will not be recognized, and securities law has been used against offers of that kind on the shallower reefs.

Common misunderstandings come from the mining news. A mining contract is a licence for a set activity for a set period, and it gives no ownership of the seabed. A US permit, if issued, would not make the patch American. The ISA's installation rules do not clearly reach a habitat with no mining, and that gap gives no permission, since Article 137 still bars taking any part of the floor as one's own.

The most workable activity is to take part in the system. A company can seek a sponsoring member country and an exploration contract, or a research group can work from a flagged ship under its flag country's law. Since 17 January 2026, members of the BBNJ Agreement, a treaty on marine life outside national waters, must also assess planned activities under their jurisdiction or control in these areas before authorising them. What it gains is a contract right to explore. It gains no land, no people under its own law and no legal basis for a state.
essays.airborne-habitats:
The idea of living permanently in the air appears in films and in architects' drawings, and it has never been done. Nobody lives on a flying platform today. To understand why, it helps to look at the machines that come closest and at the rules they already answer to.

The closest machines are called high-altitude platforms. These are uncrewed aircraft or airships meant to stay very high up for weeks or years, usually to carry radio equipment, so that they work a little like a very low satellite. The International Telecommunication Union, or ITU, is the UN agency that coordinates radio use, and its definition is the nearest thing to a legal description of these craft. Paragraph 1.66A of its Radio Regulations defines a high-altitude platform station as a radio station on an object at 20 to 50 kilometres up, at a specified nominal fixed point relative to the Earth. That wording covers radio use only. It says nothing about who owns the air at that height, and it treats the platform as a piece of radio equipment.

Those heights lie above normal traffic. In the United States, Class A airspace, the controlled airspace used by airliners, ends at 60,000 feet, about 18 kilometres, and these platforms fly above it. The air above 60,000 feet is itself classed as Class E airspace in the United States, so it remains inside the American classification system. Above Class A there is no special legal zone. Air over a country falls under that country's rules, and no treaty sets the height where this ends. No case of anyone claiming a flying nation appears in the published descriptions of these programs.

The history of the hardware explains the physical side. Helios, a NASA solar aircraft, reached 96,863 feet on 13 August 2001 and broke up in flight in 2003. The Airbus Zephyr, a solar drone, can fly for 64 days. Facebook's Aquila drone was halted in 2018, Google's Loon balloons ended in 2021, and Titan Aerospace's Solara was shut down by 2017. Other craft named in this height band include the BAE PHASA-35 and the Kea Atmos Mk1. All of these carry equipment. None carries a person to live on.

Stratobus is the project most like a long-stay habitat, and it shows how slowly such a thing moves. It is a robotic airship designed by the French company Thales Alenia Space to hover about 20 kilometres up. In 2015 the design was 100 metres long, weighed about 5 tons and could carry 250 kilograms of equipment for five years. The company expected a couple of days on the ground each year for maintenance. It planned a prototype in 2018 or 2019 and commercial sale around 2020, and neither date was met. By 2025 it was described as 142 metres long, the company had started building two reduced-scale test models, and the aim was to be ready for use by 2031. The carrying limit matters here. A payload of 250 kilograms on a craft that large is less than the weight of three or four adults, before counting food, water, air supply or walls. It carries no people, and none are planned.

Sky Cruise is the famous picture of the opposite end. It is an animated video that Hashem Al-Ghaili released in mid-2022, based on a design by art director Tony Holmsten drawn more than a decade earlier. It shows a nuclear-powered flying hotel carrying up to 5,000 people and staying in the air for years, with passengers and supplies arriving on jets that land on it. Al-Ghaili suggested that small reactors expected in the 2030s might power it. Viewers questioned its aerodynamics and whether it could fly at all, and he himself stressed that it is only a concept. No such aircraft has been built.

Suppose someone did build a crewed platform and wanted to run it as an independent place. The bumps would come in this order. Before takeoff, the craft needs safety certification and flight permission. Stratobus's makers said flight tests had to come before certification and flight authorisation, and that was for a craft with nobody aboard. Certificates come from a country, and that country's aviation authority answers for the craft. In practice, a platform answers to the aviation and radio authorities that certify it. An aircraft must be registered with a country to have legal standing under the Chicago Convention, the treaty on international civil flying, and the registering country's rules follow it.

Next come radio frequencies. A platform needs them to talk to the ground and to run any business, and frequency assignments reach the ITU through a member country, which puts that member's regulator in charge. A group with no member country behind it would have no one to file for it. Then comes the question of where the craft is. Over a country, it is in that country's air and subject to its orders. Over open ocean, no one owns the air, but the craft still carries its register's law.

After that come the physical limits. Even a platform designed for years in the air has to come down somewhere for maintenance, as Stratobus does for a couple of days a year. A place with people on it would have far greater needs, including food, water, medicine and a way to bring a sick person down. Each of those runs through an airfield in some country. Whoever controls that airfield controls the supply, which is the same weakness seen in Camp Barneo, the Arctic tourist camp that depended on Norwegian flights. Insurance, money and banking would then present the same problems as any other place outside a recognized state. A flying place with no recognized government could not license a bank, and its residents would remain citizens of their home countries, subject to their tax laws.

The business side has its own record. Several programs ended with large companies behind them, including Loon, which Alphabet closed in 2021 because it lacked a viable business. Those programs carried only equipment, with no food, water, air or medical care to pay for.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. One is that a height above airliner traffic is a height above the law. Class A ending at 60,000 feet only marks where one airspace class stops and another, Class E, begins. In February 2023 American fighters shot down a Chinese balloon at about that height. The other is that a video of a flying city means someone is building one. Sky Cruise is an animation, and the design for it has not moved past that.

The workable version today is an uncrewed platform flown with a government's permission, carrying radio or observation equipment, on a register, using licensed frequencies. No crewed flight has been reported for these programs. A permanent home in the air remains unbuilt, and estimates for it are low on building, on law and on holding the position, because the craft would need a state's registration and somewhere to land or receive supplies.
essays.host-state-carve-outs:
A country can, if it chooses, set aside part of its own land and give it different rules. It might have separate business courts, lower taxes, its own regulators or even a form of self-government. This is the one route to separate rules that starts with the consent of the government in charge, and that is why it has actually worked. The host country keeps full authority unless it gives the land away by treaty, and the grant usually comes through its ordinary laws. What one legislature grants, a later court or legislature may take back. A person who follows this route is making an arrangement with a government and accepting that government's final word.

The best working example is the Dubai International Financial Centre, a business district of 110 hectares in the United Arab Emirates. In 2004 a federal law allowed each emirate to set up legal structures for financial centres, and Dubai then passed one law creating the centre and another creating its courts, which began working in 2006. Inside the zone, civil and commercial cases follow common law, the English system built on past court rulings, and they are heard in English, apart from the rest of the country's legal system. The centre has its own financial regulator and offers companies a 50-year guarantee of zero tax on corporate income. Other laws, such as criminal law and immigration rules, still apply. It is a place to do business under different commercial rules, and it remains part of Dubai.

Honduras shows the other end of the range. In 2013 the country changed its constitution to allow Zones for Employment and Economic Development, known as ZEDEs, areas with their own laws, courts and taxes. An earlier plan had already been struck down as a breach of sovereignty, the country's right to govern itself. Próspera, on the island of Roatán, applied in 2017. It was built with American venture capital through a Delaware company that holds a veto on its council, and it offers single-digit taxes, its own regulations and a court of retired Arizona judges who hear cases online. Neighbours in the village of Crawfish Rock feared losing their land. Then politics changed. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal of the ZEDE law in April 2022, and on 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court declared the laws unconstitutional, with retroactive effect, according to Reuters.

Próspera's response shows what a company can do when a host reverses itself. It turned to treaty arbitration, in which a panel of arbitrators decides a dispute between an investor and a country. Its owners relied on a promise of stable rules and on CAFTA-DR, a trade treaty between the United States and Central American countries, and brought a claim at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), a World Bank body. The claim began at about $10.775 billion. Honduras's Attorney General says it has dropped to $1.63 billion, a cut of about 85 percent. Honduras left ICSID in August 2024 and rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026. The case was still pending in October 2026, and the zone continues to operate during the dispute. An arbitration panel can award money. It cannot give a company back the power to make law on Honduran soil.

At the far end of the range sit two old cases that did produce something close to a state. Vatican City, 44 hectares inside Rome, came from the Lateran Treaty of 1929 between Italy and the Holy See, the government of the Catholic Church. The treaty recognised the Holy See's full sovereignty over the new state and settled a dispute that had lasted about 60 years, since Italian forces took Rome in 1870. The Holy See is a non-member observer state at the UN, alongside the State of Palestine. This depended on a global church and on a government that wanted to settle with it. The Sovereign Order of Malta, a Catholic order, describes itself as sovereign and reported relations with 111 countries in 2021, and it has no land except what others let it use. A new founder has neither background.

Other carve-outs are based on long custom. Mount Athos in Greece, 335 square kilometres with 20 Orthodox monasteries, governs itself under Greek law, with the monks controlling entry through a permit system. Sark, in the Channel Islands, held on to a feudal government granted in 1565 until the billionaire Barclay brothers challenged it under the European Convention on Human Rights, and a new constitution replaced it in 2008. Cherán in Mexico threw out loggers, police and politicians in 2011, and a federal Electoral Tribunal ruling that November backed its request to choose leaders by custom.

Freetown Christiania in Copenhagen shows how such room can be won from below. Squatters moved into old barracks in 1971, and the Supreme Court ruled in 1978 that the site should be cleared, an order that was never carried out. Parliament legalised the community in 1989. A 2004 Act reaffirmed the state's control, and the Supreme Court confirmed the state's full right of disposal in February 2011. So the community lost in court and then bargained. It agreed that June to set up a fund, and in July 2012 residents became legal owners of about 19 of the 84 acres. In 2013 Parliament repealed the special Christiania law, leaving the same laws as the rest of Denmark. Residents and authorities dug up the main dealing lane, Pusher Street, in 2024 after repeated shootings, which unlocked state money, and in February 2026 residents reluctantly accepted a public housing plan. About 900 people live there, half a million people visit each year, and Danish law applies.

Many announced zones have never been built, which is the common pitfall for people who invest in them. Akon City in Senegal, which its promoter said had 2,000 acres from the president, carried a $6 billion price tag, and in 2025 the state agency that controlled the land said the project no longer exists. Bitcoin City in El Salvador relied on a $1 billion bond, and a later deal with the International Monetary Fund undercut the bitcoin policy behind it. It is not known to have been built. Forest City in Malaysia received a Special Financial Zone in 2024 after its Chinese developer ran into debts, with just over 1 percent of the development thought to be inhabited by one 2024 report. The Maldives Floating City was signed in 2010 and signed again in 2019, and finished homes have not been confirmed.

The same approach seems able to work at sea. Article 60(1) of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea says a coastal country may authorise artificial islands and installations in its exclusive economic zone, the belt of ocean where it controls resources. A floating city could therefore have a host's permission, on that host's terms. The Seasteading Institute and the government of French Polynesia signed a memorandum on 13 January 2017 for a floating prototype with legal semi-autonomy in the territory's waters. After a local presidential election changed the politics, the territory cut ties on 14 March 2018.

Suppose a group wants to do this today. It would need a government with a reason to agree, usually jobs or investment, and a law that its courts will uphold. It would ask for the grant to be written into the constitution, for a long promise of stable rules, and for a treaty that allows arbitration if the promise is broken, and Honduras shows that even a constitutional change can be undone. It would need to deal early with neighbours, because local land fears fed the opposition in Honduras. Its residents would keep their nationalities, and their home countries would go on taxing them where their laws do so. Banks would rely on the host's regulators, which is why a real regulator matters. This is the most workable route to separate courts and tax rules, with roughly even odds of building and funding it and somewhat under even odds of holding it through later elections. The zone stays part of the host country, so it does not produce recognition as a separate state.
essays.combo-religious-status:
Religious bodies have held land under special rules for centuries, and governments often treat them with care. This route asks whether a religious identity can add to a territorial claim, through a state's respect for a church, through a tax exemption, or through a religious community running its own town. It combines a host's carve-out, a takeover of local government, and a long-standing authority that does not rest on territory.

Three famous cases are often quoted, and each differs from what a new founder would have. Vatican City became a state in 1929, when Italy recognised the Holy See's sovereignty over 44 hectares in the Lateran Treaty, after a dispute lasting about 60 years. The Holy See had been a ruler and a diplomatic presence for centuries, and it has no modern imitator. Mount Athos in Greece has monks who govern a 335-square-kilometre peninsula, with monasteries dating back to at least the 9th century, under Greek law and with a church link to the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. It stays part of Greece. The Order of Malta has diplomatic relations with more than 110 countries, and it signed a treaty with Malta in 1998 for part of Fort St Angelo. Its origins go back to about 1099. Age and the consent of states are what these three share.

The law in the United States is clear in one direction. The Constitution bars government from establishing a religion, and the Supreme Court has applied that to local power. In Larkin v. Grendel's Den in 1982 it struck down a Massachusetts law letting churches veto liquor licences nearby. In Board of Education of Kiryas Joel v. Grumet in 1994 it struck down a New York statute that created a special school district following the lines of a village of Satmar Hasidim. Four justices wrote that this delegated state power to a group defined by common religion, and the Court's majority held that the law went beyond accommodating religion. A state may not hand civic authority to a group chosen by a religious test.

Here comes the point that is more open. Kiryas Joel's village itself was formed under New York's general village law, with boundaries drawn to take in only Satmars, and the Court's decision was aimed at the special school statute. Rajneeshpuram went further. The followers of Bhagwan Rajneesh bought 64,281 acres in Oregon in 1981 for $5.75 million and voted a city into being in May 1982. Oregon's attorney general argued that a city whose land and government lay with one religious group merged church and state. A federal judge ruled against the city in 1985, too late to matter, because criminal cases had ended the commune. Oregon courts later ruled in the city's favour, and when that litigation closed in 1987 the city was empty, bankrupt and legal under Oregon law. So a religious community can use general laws to form a town, and a court may then ask how far government and religion have fused. Courts decide that by the facts, and the line is not exact.

Colorado City in Arizona, with Hildale over the Utah border, shows the facts of a fusion over decades. A real estate trust of the Fundamentalist Latter-day Saints owned most of the land, and the town was incorporated in 1985. Arizona and Utah began dismantling the church's ownership in 2007. In July 2012 the Justice Department sued, saying the town government and police were taking orders from the church. In 2014 a jury found the towns had discriminated against a family that were not members and awarded $5.2 million. The population fell from 4,821 in 2010 to 2,478 in 2020.

Follow how it plays out for a new religious founder. Registering as a church may bring tax exemption, depending on the country, and it does not bring territory. The community buys land and is subject to zoning and building law. If it forms a municipality, its officers must serve everyone, and non-members who move in have rights, as the jury's award to a non-member family in Colorado City showed. Children raise special concerns for child welfare authorities, who keep their full power within religious communities. Citizenship, passports and taxes on members stay with their home countries.

Reading the record, it seems that religious status can win patience from a government and that it cannot substitute for the government's consent. That patience can be real. Greek law's treatment of Athos and Italy's treaty with the Holy See show what a very old religious institution can keep. Outside the United States, a state with an official religion could in principle grant a religious body far more than American law would allow, and this has not been tried for a new group in modern times.

The strongest version is a community that keeps its religious life private, forms no government, and owns land as a charity or company under ordinary law. It can then build a very separate way of life and last for generations, as Mount Athos shows at the far end. Recognition as a state is possible for the Holy See only because of a history no new group has.
